II. GREED, EVIL, CONFRONTATION, AND HOPE (2:1–13)


Micah 2 contains three units (2:1–5, 6–11, 12–13) that share a common theme, yet each part exhibits distinctive characteristics that distinguish it from the surrounding verses. The sequence of the first two units serves a rhetorical purpose of condemning the social oppression created by the king and the wealthy who are taking land from other Judeans. The third represents a message of hope for restoration in the midst of judgment.

One must pay careful attention to the stylistically constructed rhetoric of the passage since the speaker, genre, and time frame of the actions constantly change, even though the person, gender, and number of the speaker may not. For example, in 2:1–5, a prophetic narrator begins the passage (2:1–3aα) and formally introduces Yahweh as the next speaker. Yahweh’s first-person speech begins immediately thereafter concerning this family. Next, he addresses the same group directly using second-person masculine plural forms (you in 2:3b, 4a). Yahweh’s speech then transitions into a pronouncement of punishment that one expects in a judgment oracle. Yahweh introduces one of those lamenting in the future (masculine singular verb in 2:4a) before quoting that person’s speech (2:4b [plus the last two Hebrew words of 2:4a]). This lament refers to the loss of family land, which has now transpired, but the action being described will take place in the future. Micah 2:5 assumes the lamenter’s quotation ceases, and the prophetic narrator resumes as the communicating voice. Yahweh pronounces the punishment of the future lamenter using second-person masculine singular suffix on a preposition (ləkā). Hence, these verses use first-, second-, and third-person speech as well as singular and plural forms. The alternation seems deliberate, reflecting a poetic style that repeats key elements with slightly varied wording. At the same time, one must distinguish between Yahweh as the “I” who speaks in 2:3a, 4aα from the future lamenter who speaks about “we” (2:4aβ), “our,” “I,” and “my” (all in 2:4b). The former begins the verdict of Yahweh’s judgment oracle against the perpetrators of injustice while the latter articulates the plaintive call of someone in the future who has experienced the execution of Yahweh’s judgment. Together the two speeches pronounce imminent judgment while describing the horrific effects that the unjust will feel once Yahweh begins the actual punishment.

The second portion (2:6–11) of this larger unit (2:1–13) begins with a speaker addressing a group directly using both second-person masculine plural verbs and talking about a group using third-person plural verbs. Importantly, the change is not a random artistic variation, but an integral part of the rhetorical logic because the speaker issues negative commands to one group about another group in the present time. The meaning of the verbs, however, concerns the speech of the groups that suggests the words being spoken by one group are condemned by the one speaking, and that the current speaker makes that condemnation known to the other group. Sorting out the identities of these two groups remains a crucial exegetical task for this unit.

The third section (2:12–13) offers a promise to Jacob/Israel. Yahweh clearly speaks, but Yahweh promises to gather them together like sheep and to restore them to a bountiful land so that the sheep fill the land again. This promise, it has often been argued, offers hope to those who have been removed from the land, and thus probably reflects life after the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BCE, long after the lifetime of the prophet or Hezekiah, the Judean king most likely responsible for the reallocation of land in the Shephelah toward the end of the eighth century BCE. Hezekiah died in 696 BCE, more than a century prior to Jerusalem’s destruction. Not surprisingly, therefore, scholars have long treated these verses as a later addition to the book designed to provide hope and to affirm Yahweh’s good intentions for Yahweh’s people.

Widespread agreement exists among scholars regarding the dating of the component parts of 2:1–13. The first two sections (2:1–5, 6–11) are routinely read against the backdrop of the late eighth century, and most interpret the speeches as either composed by the prophet Micah or at least reflecting the memory of speeches delivered by the prophet. In particular, the first unit (2:1–5) confronts and condemns one group of powerful Judeans who are seizing the land of their own countrymen, with at least the implicit, if not explicit, support of the king. This situation correlates well with two pieces of data regarding the last decade of the eighth century BCE: Hezekiah’s attempt to buttress the defense of Jerusalem and Judah by fortifying the Shephelah and the fact that the prophet Micah came from the region in question (since he was born in Moresheth-Gath). Accounts of Hezekiah’s reign specify several public works projects whose purpose appears to be to strengthen Judah’s ability to fight off intruders on its western side and Jerusalem’s ability to endure a siege.1 Archaeological artifacts suggest a dramatic increase of Jerusalem’s population during the approximate time of the prophet, even if debates about the reasons for the increased infrastructure are not fully settled.2 In Mic 2, the first unit articulates divine displeasure at the upheaval caused by those who scheme to take the land of other Judeans (2:2) while the second unit condemns a group for not doing more to change the lawless behavior. Both segments anticipate Judah will not escape punishment.

The last two verses reflect a very different message and setting. Rather than continue to confront the prophet’s immediate audience, these verses speak hopefully about a return from exile. They offer a message of restoration to those in the future who have experienced divine judgment. This change from judgment to restoration represents a noticeable characteristic of the book of Micah. Chapters 4–5 and 6–7 offer similar dramatic changes. For this reason, most scholars see these verses as part of an exilic expansion to the book of Micah that helped to create the vacillation of judgment and hope that dominates the final form of the book. This alternation of judgment and hope seeks to reinforce the polarity of the prophetic message: the need for accountability of ethical and cultic expectations tempered with Yahweh’s grace and mercy toward those in Zion.





A. WOE TO THE STRONG OPPRESSING THE WEAK (2:1–5)


1Woe to those contemplating wickedness and doing evil while lying in their beds. Then they do it in the morning light because it is in their powera to do so.

2And sob they desire fields, and snatch (them).c They desired houses and take them.e They oppress a manf and his household; and they oppressg each one and his inheritance.

3Therefore, thus says Yahweh: Behold, I am contemplating evil upon this family that you will not remove from your necks. You will not walk around haughtily,h because it is an evil time.

4On that day, a taunti will be raised over you and there will be lamentation. Someone will say: “We are utterly destroyed. He has changed the allotted portionj of my people. How he has removed what belongedk to me. He has apportioned our fields to the one returning.”l

5Therefore, there will not be anyone stretching a line for you with a lot in the assembly of Yahweh.

a. The MT uses an unusual idiom (yeš ləʾēl yādām; “there is power in their hand”) to indicate “power” using the word ʾēl (which also means “god”). The idiom occurs in other texts in both a positive (Gen 31:29) and a negative (Deut 28:32; Neh 5:5) sense. The idiom confuses the LXX translator who understands the word ʾēl as “god” and translates the particle yeš as coming from the verb nśʿ (“to lift”). The translator renders the phrase with another idiom “to lift their hands to God.” In so doing, however, the translator also had to negate the phrase for it to make sense in the context. Hence the reading in the LXX (“because they did not raise their hands to God”) translates the MT loosely to fit the context. Mur 88 (an unpointed Hebrew text from the Judean Desert from 100–150 CE) confirms the MT consonants as well (see introduction to Micah in this commentary). This scroll contains the Twelve in unpointed Hebrew and agrees very closely with the MT, suggesting the move toward standardization of the Hebrew text was well underway by that time.3

b. The perfect with the vav-consecutive here designates what follows as the consequence of the preceding verse. See GKC §112 and the commentary below.

c. The verb gzl can be used intransitively elsewhere as MT has it here, but for English style it works better to add a direct object that MT implies. The LXX supplies another direct object, “orphans,” but this appears to be contextually determined, not the sign of another text. The insertion of “orphans” shows signs of contextual reflection, since the verse condemns the oppression of families and their inheritance. Mur 88 agrees with MT.

d. The verb “desire” is presumed from the first portion of the verse (ḥmd), as happens frequently in Hebrew poetry.4 Adele Berlin designates the omission of the verb in the second parallel line as the gapping of the verb and illustrates the phenomenon with Lam 5:11. Gapping can be interpreted synonymously, but the second line typically expands the meaning of the first.

e. The insertion of the direct object is provided for reasons of English style and is not present in the MT. The verb here is translated idiomatically as take, even though the verb (nśʾ) literally means “raise,” because it is used in other places to mean “take away” or “remove” (e.g., Judg 21:23; 16:31; Hos 5:14).

f. While the Hebrew word (geber) used here can certainly be used generically, and in this sense is roughly synonymous with ʾādām or ʾîš, that does not mean the word is semantically identical. The word geber conveys the sense of strength, military prowess, and dignity in a way that other words do not. See the literary discussion in the comments below.

g. The MT has no verb here, but as with the first two versets, the assumption makes sense that the verb of the first parallel verset carries over into the second. The LXX also adds the verb (“to plunder”) from the first line here for the same reason.

h. The LXX translates the Hebrew word rômâ (“exalted,” “arrogant”) with the phrase orthoi exaiphnēs (“upright speedily”) so that the resulting pronouncement “you will not walk upright quickly” builds upon the first part of the verse wherein the calamity that Yahweh will send will descend upon their necks. The image of a yoke around the neck probably caused the translator to understand rômâ to mean “exalted, high,” and thus to translate for the sense that they will not walk normally (upright). The translator then adds “speedily” to emphasize the crippling effect of the calamity, even upon their posture. The LXX thus derives from the MT, but translates loosely to make sense of the Hebrew.

i. The Hebrew word māšāl can mean a pithy saying or a parable, but when the saying is negative, it can also imply a taunt. The LXX translates with “parable,” which does not really convey the idea of taunting; the English word taunt here captures the negative element better.

j. Concerning the expression to change the allotted portion, see commentary below.

k. Literally, MT reads: “How he removed to me.” Something must be added for the verse to make sense in English. Most English translations insert “it” as an unstated object and translate lî as “from me,” but the word lî can mean “belonging to me” which makes better sense referring to the tract of the previous clause.

l. This last clause in the quoted speech remains ambiguous because the word šôbēb can be understood in two very distinct ways to mean “the one returning” or “an apostate.” Those opting for the former usually assume this verse represents a later setting from the early postexilic period. Those opting for the latter generally treat the word as a synonym for the speaker’s enemy.

The first unit of the chapter breaks down into two subunits, a judgment oracle (2:1–3) and its chronological extension (2:4–5). The judgment oracle in 2:1–3 begins like a woe oracle and condemns those in Judah who spend their nights dreaming up new ways to increase their power at others’ expense and then use their days to implement those plans. As with many judgment oracles, this description of the current situation also serves as an accusation. Micah 2:2 concretizes the nature of these schemes that threaten property distribution and the social order of families. Micah 2:3 begins with therefore, a genre marker that typically introduces the verdict in judgment oracles, as it does here. Nevertheless, the verdict contains something of a surprise in that while the accusations assume that there are perpetrators and victims in the present time, the verdict of 2:3 describes punishment for this family and thus assumes judgment will befall the entire community, whereas 2:4–5 speak about the punishment that will occur in a more distant future.

1 The opening word of 2:1, woe, evokes the somber tone of a funeral and immediately signals to the reader the judgmental rhetoric to follow. This word, when used in prophetic oracles, frequently precedes a participle describing the actions of the person or persons acting contrary to Yahweh’s expectations. Such is certainly the case in Mic 2:1–2. In 2:1, two plural participles convey the portrait of a systemic problem in which a group completely, efficiently, and continually perpetrates wickedness for their own ends. Trouble will befall those who hatch schemes at night: those contemplating wickedness and doing evil while lying in their beds. Nevertheless, their wicked behavior is ongoing. They contrive their plans at night and execute them in the light of day. The subtle shift in the parallel expressions should not be missed. The prophet condemns the schemers for planning what they will do (contemplating wickedness) as well as executing those plans (doing evil) while lying on their beds at night. This additional phrase serves to condemn them further since it implies that they enjoy what they do. They plot their actions, and they dream of carrying out those plans. The double condemnation emphasizes the dastardly seriousness of their actions (wicked/evil), but it also articulates the unrelenting severity of the actions as happening around the clock. The schemes are hatched at night and executed by day (in the morning light), implying this evil does not stop. These people behave immorally but they appear to have some level of authorization to do what they do since the prophet implies that the motivation for their actions derives simply from their having the power to do what they want to do.

This group does not appear to represent the actions of some marginalized faction of society. Rather, according to 2:1b this group executes its plans with impunity merely because it has the power to do so. Given the assumption that Mic 2 should be heard against the background of the end of the eighth century BCE, and that Micah himself may have been an elder of one of the Judean hill country towns, it is no wonder that scholars have speculated that the identity of the group in question must in some way be related to a politically powerful group, presumably even one related closely to the Judean monarchy. Furthermore, scholars suggest that the group to which this text alludes may have been those responsible for carrying out the reforms of Hezekiah that involved consolidating and centralizing the power of the king in Jerusalem.5

2 The nature of the plans becomes clearer in 2:2, and the actions described in this verse imply that the group responsible for implementing these plans is an inner Judean group, not an external power. Micah 2:2 contains two pairs of parallel versets describing the violent actions of those seizing property (A1–2) and the consequences these actions have for the families affected (B1–2). These four versets thus create two lines with their own internal parallelism, but the two lines are also linked thematically in reverse order with 2:2a dealing with the violent takeover of fields/houses and 2:2b dealing with the implications of the loss of these same items.

A1And so they desire fields [śādeh], and snatch (them).

A2(They desire) houses [bāyit] and take them.

B1They oppress a man [geber] and his household [bāyit];

B2and (they oppress) each one [ʾiyš] and his inheritance [naḥălâ].

The logical connection between these two lines is clear: to expose and condemn the cause-and-effect relationship between unchecked power and suffering. Lines A1–2 describe the brutality and callousness of a powerful group that does as they please. They see something they want, and they take it. Lines B1–2 also revolve around the effects of their actions, but these lines focus upon the consequences for the victims. The double mention of house(s) in A2 and B1 links the two thematic parts. The two lines draw upon multiple connotations of the Hebrew word bāyit and underscore the fact that a house is not merely a building. Rather, a house (bāyit) constituted the dwelling place of an entire family unit, a household (also a meaning of bāyit), which has their homestead confiscated. The double mention of bāyit (“house”) also follows a typical pattern in Hebrew parallelism involving an intensification from the first to the second.6 They take houses (A2) but in so doing they oppress a landowner and his household (B1). The resulting portrait creates a poetic dichotomy in that the geber (“man”) can do nothing against the power of the oppressor.

The second portion of this parallelism between the lines may not be evident at first glance, but it makes a powerful statement, nonetheless. The first line describes the taking of fields by this powerful group, but as with the double mention of bāyit, the second part of the parallelism draws upon the consequences of the lost fields, not merely the fact that the fields were lost. The loss of land (A1) has consequences, since, in the ancient world, land constituted the inheritance that a father could pass down to his son. Thus, the logic connecting A1 with its counterpart in B2 should not be overlooked. The loss of land does not merely mean the loss of a piece of property. Rather, it creates economic and social repercussions since that man and his family will lose all food production from the field, and that man will literally be unable to leave an inheritance to the next generation.

The intertwining of parallel terms adds to the intensification of the action described in 2:2. The use of the verbs in lines A1 and A2 intensifies the action by using one verbal clause (they desire) followed by two direct objects stating the target of their desire: they desire fields … and houses. The verb “desire” here is the same root (ḥmd) typically translated as “covet” in the Decalogue (Exod 20:17), adding a powerful word that carries a heavy sense of taboo. Both lines A1 and A2 express the action of the land grabbers using two parallel verbs (snatch, take), closely associating the actions with the covetous desire: they desire … and snatch … and take. The same style appears in lines B1 and B2, except that the single ruling verb expresses the consequences of their actions on the victims using the verb oppress (ʿšq). This time, the two parts ruled by the verb each contain double direct objects, intensifying the oppressive acts: they oppress … a man and his household … each one and his inheritance. The choice of these words for the direct object also carries powerful undertones that add to the sense of intensification. The word for man (geber) is not the more common terms ʾadām or “male” (from the rook zkr). The term geber comes from the root word that means strong and virile. The pairing of geber with household thus encompasses his extended family, his genetic kin, as the ones who suffer. The actions of the land grabbers thus endanger the virility of the man they oppress, which has long-term implications. In line B2, the words paired with one another using another word for man (ʾiyš) that connotes more of a sense of the individual with the word inheritance, a word that relates to the intergenerational wealth that passes from the male to his descendants. In other words, line B1 concerns genetic longevity of the man’s familial line and B2 concerns the long-term economic stability of the extended family. These terms are more than just near synonyms. The combination of the four terms intensifies the charges against this group.

3 The judgment oracle culminates in 2:3 with the pronouncement of judgment proper. As is typical for judgment oracles, the word therefore followed by the messenger formula (thus says Yahweh) signals the beginning of the pronouncement of the punishment in judgment oracles.7 The punishment pronouncement provides a sense of poetic justice by articulating the verdict in terms reminiscent of those with which the judgment oracle began in 2:1. Since 2:1 condemned the perpetrators of oppression who contemplated wickedness and did evil, it is altogether fitting that Yahweh’s judgment will repay their actions in kind. Thus, Yahweh announces he is contemplating evil, thereby taking one element from each of the two opening accusations. The syntactical construction also conveys a sense of imminent action, wherein the particle hinnēh plus a participle accentuates the danger this pronouncement poses by stressing its imminence.8

The verdict also contains an intriguing reference to the object of this pronouncement as this family. The word translated as family (mišpāḥâ) normally refers to an extended family, or clan, but frequently refers to the entire nation as a family as well.9 Yet, within the context of Mic 2:1–3, the identity of this family as the entire nation hardly seems to fit because 2:1–2 condemns a powerful group for taking land and property from others, meaning that Yahweh’s people are divided into at least two groups. Further, the judgment proper appears to concern itself with the actions of these oppressors since it describes this family as haughty in the second half of 2:3. Given the likelihood that Hezekiah’s centralization policies involved building public projects to collect taxes and provide military fortresses, the monarchy probably would have taken over land in the Shephelah to complete some of these projects. One can thus safely assume that the identity of this oppressive family alludes to the royal family in a manner that was not terribly subtle at the time. In the context of the late eighth century BCE, this family taking the land from its owners with no legal repercussions would refer to the family of Hezekiah, the ruling monarch of Judah from 725–696 BCE. Since Micah came from Moresheth-Gath, many scholars consider him to have been one of the landowners and elders of that village. The backdrop of this judgment oracle, then, could very well be referring to the so-called reforms of Hezekiah, reforms that undoubtedly had political as well as religious implications. Later generations of the power structure in Jerusalem would have viewed these changes positively, but the landowners in the Shephelah whose land was taken would have undoubtedly had concerns. Politically, Hezekiah’s reforms in part sought to centralize the power of the kingdom of Judah in Jerusalem, an endeavor that likely involved the confiscation of properties in outlying areas to construct and/or solidify fortifications throughout the territory. These reforms may very well have involved tax increases that, at least for a time, created economic burdens for some, especially outside Jerusalem. One can well imagine that Mic 2:1–3 condemns these unilateral actions as the work of a single, royal family who leveraged the power to take fields and houses from those in the rural regions of the country to protect Jerusalem.10

The language in 2:3 implies that the punishment from Yahweh will serve as a yoke around the necks of its target. Literally, the pronouncement states that they will not be able to take their necks away from the evil Yahweh contemplates. Most commentators suggest that this image presupposes a yoke placed around the neck, since other prophetic texts use this image as well.11 This image carries over into the next line condemning the “haughty,” a word that derives from the Hebrew word meaning “high, exalted.” In 2:3bβ, the persons whose necks are burdened by the calamity Yahweh sent will no longer be able to strike the arrogant pose of those who walk with their head held high. The arrogant will be humbled by being yoked to the service of another ruler. The implications of this judgment become more pronounced in 2:4–5.

4 The second section of the judgment oracle (2:4–5) represents a chronological extension of 2:1–3, essentially repeating the structure of a judgment oracle by describing the situation in terms of the enduring consequences of the verdict of 2:3. Micah 2:4 describes the future situation (beginning with the phrase on that day) while simultaneously connecting to the verdict of 2:3. In other words, 2:4 refers to the future punishment announced in 2:3 and describes the consequences of that punishment. Like 2:3, 2:5 begins with therefore, causing the reader to expect another pronouncement of judgment. Together, 2:4–5 thus mirror the structure of a judgment oracle with a description of the situation (2:4) followed by the introduction of the verdict with therefore (2:5). This verdict flows from the consequences of 2:3 where the lamenter lost his inheritance. Micah 2:5, however, does not pronounce a second judgment. Rather, it summarizes the future consequences of the judgment pronounced in 2:3. The one whose inheritance has been seized will no longer participate in the casting of lots in the Judean assembly.

Several commentators note that 2:4–5 appears to reinterpret the original setting of the judgment oracle of 2:1–3.12 For some, rather than announcing punishment for a specific group that is oppressing another group in 2:1–2, 2:4 seems to presume that the punishment here is directed against the entire nation.13 These commentators, then, often suggest that this updated reading reflected (especially) in 2:5 presumes an exilic setting wherein the specter of Jerusalem’s destruction in 587 BCE continues to dominate the theological hermeneutics of those compiling prophetic texts. This judgment oracle (2:1–3) thus becomes another example of Micah’s pronouncements of the coming destruction of Jerusalem that threatens Judah. This updated reading does not presume imminent judgment as in 2:3, but the phrase in 2:4 with which it opens (on that day) presupposes that the judgment lies in the more distant future, an interpretation made possible by the assumption that the pronouncement of judgment in 2:3 was fulfilled against Jerusalem in 587 BCE.14

Another group of commentators focuses upon the change of perspective in 2:4 that, while it presupposes knowledge of 2:3, begins with the introduction of a taunt placed in the mouth of the one being punished. This taunt acknowledges the consequences of 2:3.15 The opening of 2:4 announces that a taunt will come about in the form of a lamentation spoken by those who have been punished. The taunt proper begins with a statement acknowledging the devastation: we are utterly destroyed. The taunt thus presumes that the speaker has now changed. The speaker is now the one who has experienced the punishment announced in 2:3. The speaker acknowledges Yahweh’s punishment in this lament: He has changed the allotted portion of my people. The subject he refers to Yahweh. The word translated allotted portion (ḥēleq) typically refers to something that has been divided among a group, whether that be a soldier’s portion of the booty taken after a battle (e.g., Gen 14:24; Num 31:36) or a portion of land allocated to a people (e.g., Josh 18:5; 19:9; Hos 5:7). In the context of 2:1–3, the speaker’s statement implies a complete reversal of the situation from 2:1–2 so that the oppressor who has taken the houses and fields of others now finds himself in the situation where his own land has been taken. The fact that the word allotted portion often refers to family land also adds to the poignancy of this statement following 2:3, which announced Yahweh’s intention to punish this family.

The second half of the taunt (2:4aβ–b) continues the speech with three clauses that concretize what the utter devastation mentioned in 2:4aα means. The first clause, as already noted, announces the loss of territory belonging to my people: He has changed the allotted portion of my people. The second explanatory clause (How he has removed what belonged to me) laments the loss of land that the speaker pitifully considered to be his own. The second clause in the taunt begins with the Hebrew interrogative “How?” (ʾêk), but this word appears in contexts of lamentation to express dismay and sadness over what has happened rather than to ask a question (see 2 Sam 1:19; Isa 14:12; Ezek 26:17). In the context of Mic 2:1–2, however, this lamentation rings hollow in the mouth of the one who has taken what does not belong to him. The third explanatory clause laments that Yahweh has given this land to someone else: He has apportioned our land to one returning. This last line creates considerable ambiguity depending upon how one understands the word that functions as the object (see text note). While all agree that the word ləšôbēb stems from the root šûb (“turn,” “return”), they do not all agree on the meaning of the verb in the polel stem. Some consider the context of the lament and translate the idea of return in the sense of returning as retaliation, hence rendering the participle in MT with the idea of “the one paying back,” “corrupting,” or “repaying,” which appears in the hiphil stem (such as Exod 21:34; Deut 32:41, 43).16 Others, including my translation, understand the form in a more positive sense, the “one who restores” or “returns.”17 The quotation from the one being punished ends with this line, but the parable (or taunt) continues in 2:5 by describing the consequences of the judgment in the future.

5 The appearance of a second therefore (lākēn) in this unit appears superfluous to some who consider 2:5 to be a later interpretive comment.18 Nevertheless, this verse belongs inherently with 2:4, which specifically extends the punishment of 2:1–3 by explicating the future consequences of 2:1–3 for the guilty party.

To understand this verse, one must deduce from other contexts what it means to stretch a line … with a lot and how to identify the assembly of Yahweh. At its core, the word assembly (qāḥāl) refers to a gathered body of people, but the identity of the assembly and the reason for gathering must be determined by context. The word can be used to refer to soldiers, either of Yahweh’s people (Judg 20:2) or foreign enemies (Ezek 17:17). The assembly can refer to the gathering of people for a religious service (e.g., Joel 2:16; Ps 107:32). It can also refer to civil actions in a juridical context, for example, after a judge declares someone guilty and the assembly carries out the execution by stoning. Such a process is outlined in Ezek 23:45–47 where a formal judgment is delivered for a capital crime and the assembly carries out the sentence. Undoubtedly, other such serious judgments could require the involvement of the local assembly, and that body likely consisted of the landowners of the town. The context of Mic 2:5 could very well have some kind of formal action in mind when it refers to stretching a line.

Sweeney sees the act of stretching a line as referring to a right of land ownership while maintaining that the assembly need not refer to a religious gathering.19 He thus correctly places this verse into the context of the removal of someone from the community of landowners. To this idea, Allen provides a supplemental note in that the practice refers to the distribution of communal land that would have to be reallocated periodically.20 The image of dividing land appears with the same verb in Amos 7:17, though other verbs also describe the practice (Pss 16:6; 78:55; 2 Sam 8:2). Scholars often note that Josh 18:8, 10 may have influenced the statement in Mic 2:5 that this practice was performed by lot.21 This latter reading assumes that 2:5 refers to the redistribution of land to a group of returnees, which draws a parallel to Joshua’s allotment of the entire country to the twelve tribes in the premonarchic era. Actually, this image extends well beyond Josh 18. The command to divide the land by lot appears in Num 26:55–56, a command attributed to Moses that each tribe and each family would receive its allotted share.

55But the land shall be apportioned by lot; according to the names of their ancestral tribes they shall inherit. 56Their inheritance shall be apportioned according to lot between the larger and the smaller.

Each tribe will receive a portion, selected by lot, but each tribe’s portion will also be subdivided among the family clans by lot, using the plural of mišpāḥâ. In anticipation of the division of the territory, Num 26 refers to the families of these tribes (using the plural of mišpāḥâ) more than eighty times. The key words of Mic 2:4–5 evoke this action: the guilty party has lost his right to possess land.

In light of this conceptualization, the images in Mic 2:4–5 become clearer, and they dramatically heighten the stakes of Yahweh’s punishment in 2:1–3. The family (i.e., clan) who is currently taking the land allotted to others will themselves lose their own allotted territory. If, as seems likely, the original setting for this pronouncement was directed against the royal family, Hezekiah’s descendants, then the implications of this scenario can hardly be overstated. The prophet announces that the king’s family would lose their allotted portion, thereby implying grave danger for Jerusalem as well since that is where the king lived. Precisely this threat against Jerusalem plays a key role in both 1:2–7 and 3:9–12. The motif may be expressed more subtly in 2:1–5, but its presence conveys nothing short of a pronouncement of the end of the ruling family in Jerusalem.





B. A PROPHET DISPUTING HIS ENEMIES (2:6–11)


6You should not preacha as they preach: “Do not droolb such things.c He will not remove humiliations.”d

7Should it be said in the house of Jacob: “Has the spirit of Yahweh become impatient? Or, are these his doings? Do my words not do good to the one walking uprightly?”

8Previously, he established my people as an enemy. Prior to that,e you stripped off a splendid robef from those passing through in security, those returning from war.g

9The womenh of my people you drovei from the house of her delightsj. You removed my splendork from her childrenl forever.m

10Arise and go for this is not the resting place. Because it has become unclean, it will be destroyed and the destruction will be grievous.n

11Ifo a man walkingp after windq and falsehood lies (sayingr): “I will preachs to you for wine and liquor,” then he would be the one preaching to these people.

a. The verb nṭp appears three times in this verse (see the next textual note). The LXX translates the same text as MT, but with a very different understanding than modern English translations. The LXX translates the verb nṭp (which literally means “to drip”) with the Greek verb “to weep,” apparently interpreting the triply mentioned “dripping” as tears falling from the speaker. By contrast, most English translations rely upon other contexts (Ezek 21:2–7; Amos 7:17) to understand nṭp as a derogatory term for “preaching” (figuratively, “dripping from the mouth”). See the commentary for an explanation of the word play with these verbs.

b. The translation attempts to capture the word play in English. This verb is a hiphil imperfect from the root nṭp (meaning “to drip”), just as the previous verb translated as preach. The use of nṭp, however, carries strong negative connotations as well. It typically levels a critique about the content of what someone is saying. This third use of nṭp is thus translated as drool to convey the rhetorical barb. See the commentary for more details.

c. Ernst Sellin opts to read the consonants ʿlh to mean “curse” rather than vocalizing the word with MT as the plural pronoun, “these things.”22 To do so he also emends other words in the clause without textual evidence. It is better to struggle with MT.23

d. Contrary to several English versions, the plural noun insults must be the object of the singular niphal verb yissag (which means “to turn away” or “to become disloyal”), not the subject. The niphal verb, it should be noted, primarily conveys the sense of reflexivity, not passivity as with English passive verbs.24 See the commentary below.

e. The two words for “previously” (ʾetmôl, mimmûl) used in 2:8 imply a chronological sequence. Since the second occurrence has the preposition min (from) attached, and it represents the actions of the people that caused the antagonism implicit in 2:8a, the word mimmûl interprets the action in 2:8b as preceding the punishment announced in 2:8a. See the commentary below.

f. At least four alternatives have been suggested for the MT phrase śalmâʾeder (splendid robe). Most English translations assume that the word ʾeder in MT has omitted a tav at the end of the second word, so it would have originally been ʾadderet (“cloak,” “mantle”). Since the next word begins with a tav haplography could have occurred, but this solution seems rather convenient. The LXX treats the first word as having a shin rather than a sin in MT. That could mean that the consonants of the first word could have been šlmh, a feminine adjective (meaning “complete”), so that the MT could have originally meant “entire garment.” The adjective would normally come after the noun, however, so this translation seems unlikely. The NIV assumes the MT is correct but translates the noun ʾeder adjectivally (“rich robe”). The noun “robe” (śalmâ) is in the absolute state so the phrase cannot be translated as a construct chain (“robe of splendor”). A fourth alternative would be to assume that an original ʾadderet (“cloak”) became corrupted to ʾeder but was originally in apposition to śalmâ (“a robe, a cloak”). While none of these options can account for the text without problems, my translation assumes MT but also assumes that ʾeder must be translated adjectivally. Zechariah 11:13 uses the noun ʾeder in much the same way to refer to the “splendid price” (literally, “the splendor of the price”) paid to the prophet. The word is treated as a construct noun in that case, but it nevertheless functions as a modifier to the following noun. Despite the translation difficulties posed by the phrase, the sense is nevertheless clear that the people attacked those who should have had safe passage.25

g. The LXX of 2:8 reads quite differently: “And previously, my people resisted in hostility; contrary to his peace, they stripped off his skin.” Despite the differences, it is doubtful that the LXX presupposes a different source text. Rather, the Greek represents a translator trying to make sense of an obtuse text, and this text remains open to interpretation. The consonantal text was likely the same (or nearly so), but the LXX describes the brutality of skinning a human being (“stripped off his skin”), which fits the larger context (see 3:2–3), by apparently reading MT’s ʾeder (splendor) as ʾadderet, a variation of only a single letter in the consonantal text. This word usually means “cloak” or “mantle,” but it can also mean “skin,” “pelt,” or “hide” (Gen 25:25; Zech 13:4). The extant portions of Mur 88 agree perfectly with MT in 2:8, though small lacunae exist in one word and parts of two others. Given that this manuscript is a Hebrew text, Mur 88 gives MT a high degree of credibility. Still, the early Greek manuscript from Nahal Hever (8Ḥev 1) presents another variant reading from both the Old Greek and the MT. The translator uses slightly different Greek words in places and different case endings, presumably adopting a looser translation style in an effort to improve the readability in Greek. The lacunae in 8Ḥev 1 make it difficult to translate meaningfully, but one example may suffice. The LXX refers to the “stripping off” of the skin using a form of ekderō while 8Ḥev 1 uses a form of periballō, a verb meaning “to wrap around.” It thus seems to interpret the skin that was wrapped around the person, and likely refers to a leather coat of some kind.

h. The LXX understands the unpointed MT consonants (nšy) as nśyʾ (“leaders”), but to do so it must also change the verb from masculine and singular to feminine and plural, which seems dubious. MT is preferred. See note m below.

i. The LXX changes the verb from “you drove out” to “they were driven out” to make “leaders” fit the context. See note m below.

j. The LXX has a feminine plural, again representing a loose translation to attempt to make better sense of the phrase from the house of her delights. See note m below. The MT of the phrase is difficult since gender and number do not follow expectations. MT uses the third-person feminine singular suffix (“her”) to refer to the plural collective (“women of my people”). The fact that the third-person feminine singular suffix appears a second time in this verse makes it unlikely that this represents a copyist error. Relatedly, MT has the singular construct of “house,” which frequently appears with a plural noun but assumes multiple houses (see GKC §124r). Despite the difficulties, MT is translated here.

k. The LXX translates hārêʿôlām (“mountains of perpetuity”) rather than the MT’s hădārî ləʿôlām (“my splendor forever”). This change appears to be deliberate for the LXX translator to improve the sense of the sentence. See note m below.

l. Following MT. The LXX assumes an additional yod so that it translates MT’s ʿllyh (“her children”) as ʿlylyh (“her deeds”) but changes the pronoun from singular to plural (“their deeds”) to fit the context. Mur 88 confirms MT, which again implies the LXX translator deliberately rearranges letters to make sense of the consonants. See note m below.

m. As with 2:8, the LXX of Mic 2:9 reads quite differently than the MT, but it is not looking at a different consonantal text. The LXX translates: “Therefore, the leaders of my people shall be cast out of their homes of luxury. Because of their evil practices, they have been expelled. Draw near to the everlasting mountains” (NETS). While it is tempting to follow the LXX because it reads more smoothly, the principle of lectio difficilior likely applies here, especially since Mur 88 agrees with MT.

n. The LXX changes most of the forms of address in 2:10, again in a deliberate move to smooth the syntax: “Arise [singular] and go [singular], because this rest is not for you [singular], due to its uncleanness. You [plural] were corrupted with corruption” (NETS). The bracketed notes identify the changes from the MT that must be deliberate. Mur 88 confirms MT.

o. The MT has lû (“if,” “were it so that”) while Mur 88 has the particle of negation lôʿ (“not”). The unpointed text of the MT has a vav where Mur 88 has an aleph. The difference allows the first part of the verse in Mur 88 to read more smoothly: “No one should walk after wind and falsehood.” The Mur 88 reading is more likely an interpretive change.

p. The LXX appears to abandon the Hebrew entirely here by using two roughly synonymous verbs (katadiōkō and diōkō) where MT has only one. The LXX translation (“you were pursued, no one pursuing”) neither clarifies the MT nor offers a clue to a different text. The LXX appears to interpret this line as the conclusion to 2:10 by making pneuma (“spirit/wind”) the subject of the verb “establish.” Some English translations (e.g., NRSV, CEB) translate the first verb in 2:11, which comes from the root hlk, more metaphorically as a reference to behavior more than physical movement: “go about.” HALOT lists “behave” as a viable translation deriving from the idea of halākāh (“custom,” “rule”) based upon Isa 33:15; Ps 15:2. These translations, however, then have difficulty incorporating the word rūaḥ into the translation of Mic 2:11.

q. The LXX translates “wind” as the subject and creates an idiosyncratic combination of the next two words: “a spirit established a lie.”

r. Interpreting kizzēb as the apodosis of the “if … then” construction, and as the introduction of the quotation of the lying prophet, the word saying is inserted for clarity of English syntax.

s. The word here literally means “to drip,” but this root (nṭp) also appears to be an idiom that means “to drip at the mouth” and is used derogatorily of prophet’s speaking. See Ezek 21:2, 7; Amos 7:16; Mic 2:6. In the first two instances, the idiom even parallels the verb nbʿ (“to prophesy, proclaim”).

Micah 2:6–11 comprises the second unit of the chapter. For most commentators, it represents a prophetic disputation wherein one must pay careful attention to identify the changing speakers because sometimes the prophet speaks as the prophet to the people, while at other times (2:6b, 7 [after the first three words], 11aβ–b) the prophet quotes his opponents in order to dispute their claims.26 Complicating the interpretation of these verses is the difficulty of discerning the setting and the precise meaning of some of the phrases. Most of the ancient versions struggle with the meaning of the text and translate it based upon their understanding of words that can have multiple meanings. Hence, these versions are of little value in finding a “better” text. Commentators are also split on the issue of whether 2:6–11 represents an independent unit placed here because the reference to “these things” can be interpreted as referring to the judgment in 2:1–5,27 or whether 2:6–11 originally followed 2:1–5.28 In both cases, however, most see the unit as early material reflecting a speech of the eighth-century prophet.

Micah 2:6–11 takes on the form of a prophetic disputation. This disputation provides evidence of early resistance to the message of Micah. Those who conserved the sayings preserved the memory of a confrontation in which the prophetic speaker addresses one group about another group, sometimes quoting the contrarians to challenge their claims and sometimes speaking about them. This recorded confrontation suggests the hostile group tries to stop the prophet and his supporters from preaching (2:6). They challenge the prophet’s assumptions, while the prophet’s sayings condemn their ongoing behavior (2:7–10) and sarcastically accuse the group of wanting to buy pronouncements from those willing to preach for liquor. The intensity of the challenges and the counterclaims testifies to the strong investment by both sides in getting their respective points across. Since the imagery of the disputation concerns the content of speeches, the antagonists have regularly been identified as other prophets. It is important that one pay careful attention to the speakers and addressees to follow the rhetorical logic. The prophet strings together several accusations, though the lack of context makes it difficult to know precisely what is being alleged in places. The accusations include: the people challenging Yahweh’s messenger, ambushing travelers, and stealing their clothes; expelling women from their homes, leaving children without homes, and listening to false prophets. The prophet warns his addressees to leave because the place has become unclean. A significant number of scholars argue that the speech was delivered in the Shephelah, presumably in the prophet’s hometown, Moresheth-Gath, shortly before the Assyrians began attacking Judah.

6 The verse begins with a prophetic statement telling a group not to preach (literally, “drip”) that which they are preaching. In other words, “you should not do what they are doing.” This negative command implies that what they say is improper or false. The verb nṭp appears three times, dramatically emphasizing the improper content of what they are saying. The prophetic speaker essentially characterizes their words as that which drools from their mouths. Some commentators interpret the drool literally as the frothing of the mouth that certain ecstatic prophets produced when they communicated with the deity.29 Others try to lessen the negative connotations of the verb.30 The remainder of the verse concerns the content of the opponents’ speech, though it remains debated where the cited words of the opponents begin and end. Nevertheless, the point is clear that they admonish the prophet and his audience not to preach these things because he (meaning Yahweh) will not remove the humiliations. The context of this quote is missing, but in its current location these things most naturally refer to the judgment pronouncements in 2:1–5. The prophet’s opponents attempt to silence him by claiming he does not speak for Yahweh.

The phrase “Do not preach/drool such things” has also been interpreted variously. Some interpret the negative command as spoken by the prophet’s antagonists while others interpret the phrase as the words of the prophet to the antagonists.31 What both groups generally agree upon is that reference to these things refers to the punishments announced in 2:1–5.

The form of the verb yissag is also not easy to identify with complete satisfaction. It does not conform to normal paradigms for third-person masculine singular imperfect verbs. Consequently, the root for the verb is treated as sûg (“turn back,” “remove”) by some and nsg (“reach,” “overtake”) by others. Some translations ignore the fact that the singular verb is followed by a plural noun, which they translate as the subject. For example, the NRSV translates the verb from nsg as “disgrace will not overtake us,” even though the word humiliations is plural in the Hebrew text while the verb is singular. Conversely, the NASB translates the verb from sûg, recognizes that the word for insults or humiliations (kəlimmôt) is plural, and uses a passive construction to reflect the niphal verb form: “reproaches will not be turned back.” The MT has a third-person singular verb and so the plural insults should be interpreted syntactically as the object: “He will not … reproaches.” Once one recognizes this syntactical construction manifests an indirect accusative (see text note d above), deriving the verb from sûg (“remove”) makes the best sense: “He will not remove humiliations.” Syntactically, this is the most obvious way to read this clause, but it raises the question, who is he in this context. Since the previous line refers to “these things” to speak about the punishment from Yahweh, the most likely subject would be Yahweh. In a number of cases the word humiliation refers to the consequences of improper action by a person or a group.32 The word humiliations refers to the aftermath of the punishment announced in 2:1–5, and 2:6 affirms Yahweh’s intention to implement those actions. The phrase mirrors the theological presupposition that one finds in the oracles against the nations in Amos 1–2: “for three transgressions of X, and for four, I will not take it back.” A prophetic judgment, once issued, could only be removed by Yahweh, but Yahweh would expect to see changes of behavior and of attitude on the part of the wrongdoers (see Joel 2:12–14).

7 This verse contains a series of confrontational rhetorical questions that assume that the speaker claims the authority to speak on behalf of the deity to condemn the theology of the other group. Unfortunately, debate remains over the identity of the speaker(s). The majority argue that Micah uses a dispute style to pose these rhetorical questions to counter the challenge from those articulating the antagonistic response to the prophet’s speech.33 Not all agree, however, since some scholars attribute the speaker in 2:7a to the words of the prophet’s antagonists that belong more closely to 2:6.34 At least one recent commentator argues that the issue will not likely ever be resolved for two reasons: (1) both groups are claiming divine sanction for their positions; and (2) at least the last question makes sense in the mouth of either party because its theological stance is utterly dismissive of those with conflicting views.35 The majority opinion works best because the rhetorical questions fit the disputation style, but one should recognize the ambiguous nature of the claims because both sides presuppose Yahweh is on their side of the debate.

The prophet identifies the house of Jacob as the recipient of Yahweh’s message. The prophet’s counteroffensive begins with three rhetorical questions designed to underscore Yahweh’s message to the oppressors and to challenge them to consider how they should respond. Rhetorical questions presume one knows the answer, and in the case of the three questions posed by the prophet, the answer one should presume is “yes” for each question. Has the spirit of Yahweh become impatient? Yes. The prophet must challenge the activities of the oppressors (2:1–5) because these activities are contrary to the behavior Yahweh expects. Are these Yahweh’s doings? Yes. This question assumes that nothing happens without Yahweh’s knowledge. The actions Yahweh intends to take have been communicated to the oppressors as a warning to change their behavior. Do my words not help the righteous? Yes. The key to understanding the third question comes in identifying the prophet as the speaker. The prophetic voice is clear in the first two questions, and there is no convincing reason for seeing the third question as coming from another speaker. Rather, my words must refer to the prophet’s own words, and there can be little doubt that those who placed 2:6–11 in its current location must have understood 2:1–5 as the words to which this question refers.36 In so doing, this third question conveys the sense of purpose for 2:1–5. The judgment announced there should serve as an admonition to change for anyone who considered themselves to be found among those who walk uprightly.

The word translated as impatient in the first question comes from the root qṣr II. This verb conveys the basic meaning “to be short.” Most lexicons of Biblical Hebrew distinguish qṣr II (“to be short”) as a distinct entry from qṣr I (“to harvest”), but the two verbs may be conceptually linked. The process of harvesting grains would involve cutting the grain to pile in sheaves, which are then taken to be beaten in order to remove the grain from the heads. The portion left in the ground would, therefore, be that which had been cut off. This part of the plant would simply become part of the soil for the next crop.

The third question presupposes a relational theology in which Yahweh’s actions—even those that seem punitive—are assumed to have good intentions. The idiom of the phrase do good to appears in three other places where the preposition marks the recipient of the good actions (Gen 32:9, 12; Num 10:32). The theological paradigm assumed by the statement appears prominently in Jer 7:23 and 29:11.

But this command I gave them, “Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk only in the way that I command you, so that it may be well with you.” (Jer 7:23 NRSV, emphasis added)

Even when Yahweh announces that he will exile those in Jerusalem to Babylon for seventy years, this punishment is framed as a necessary reset to the relationship:

10 For thus says the LORD: Only when Babylon’s seventy years are completed will I visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise and bring you back to this place. 11 For surely I know the plans I have for you, says the LORD, plans for your welfare and not for harm, to give you a future with hope. (Jer 29:10–11 NRSV, emphasis added)

It is in this light that the final question of Mic 2:7 should be heard. Those walking uprightly will benefit from the words of Yahweh, even if those words announce corrective measures to be taken against those who are acting inappropriately.

One can sense a contrasting parallel between the judgment announced in 2:3 and the portrayal of the ideal response implied by 2:7. The judgment pronouncement in 2:3 essentially portrays the bringing low of the haughty (“high-minded”) by encumbering them with a burden around their neck so they cannot walk upright. The third rhetorical question in Mic 2:7, by contrast, implies that the threatened judgment will benefit those who wish to walk uprightly. Even the rhetoric of the wording in 2:3 and 2:7 offers contrasting views of how one should walk. In 2:3, the word translated as “haughty” implies a person who is high and exalted, but the word, rômâ, has a decidedly sarcastic tone. By contrast, 2:7 refers to walking uprightly using the word yāšār which means upright and proper.37 The contrasting images work well together since the judgment saying in 2:3 announces that Yahweh will cause those who consider themselves above their neighbors to become stooped over from the burden Yahweh will send, while the rhetorical question in 2:7 implies that those who “walk uprightly” will benefit from the prophet’s corrective words.

8 Micah 2:8–9 renews the accusations against the group whom the prophet confronts. The prophet levels charges against the group of oppressors who have performed egregious acts of brutality and intimidation. The speaker claims that previously, he established my people as an enemy. The precise circumstances of this accusation remain clouded in obscurity, though the prophet clearly addresses a group, because the prophet uses the verb stripped off (pšṭ) in the plural to accuse the group: you stripped off a splendid robe. The prophet also confronts the actions of one group against another group that was innocent when the oppressors took advantage of them. It is unclear whether this second group is the same group the speaker calls my people, but this interpretation appears most likely. The prophet confronts a group that has robbed the clothes from people who should have had safe passage after fighting in a war. The two words previously (ʾetmûl) and prior to that (mimmûl) seem to assume that the oppressors attacked the prophet’s people who subsequently became hostile to the oppressors. Given that both groups represent Judeans, one can imagine that the prophet stands up for a group in Moresheth-Gath (or the broader Judean hill country) that has been mistreated. In other words, retaliation creates a circle of violence.

While a significant number of interpreters interpret the antagonistic group who challenge the prophet as other prophets whose sympathies lie with the Judean monarch, less agreement exists about identifying the groups to whom Micah refers. Someone established my people as an enemy, but we are not told the identity of this person. The vast majority imagine that the enemy group is in some way connected to the king’s representatives who were executing the centralization policies of Hezekiah, but doing so in a way that benefited themselves while treating those whose land was dispossessed in the harshest of ways.38 Some interpret the enemy as Judeans taking advantage of those fleeing Assyria when Sennacherib began his march toward Jerusalem.39 Others suggest that the stripping refers to the treatment of prisoners of war, and thus at least implicitly set the stage in a similar way.40 Relatedly, Yahweh could also be the intended subject of the verb he established.41 At any rate, the prophet sides with the victims and excoriates those who take advantage of them.

9 The prophet continues to level charges against these oppressors but adopts the voice of Yahweh to speak about my people and my glory. Micah 2:9 charges the oppressors with expelling women and children from their homes. The wording of this verse is complex. The first accusation concerns the women of my people. The prophet accuses the oppressors of driving women and children from their homes, but the wording emphasizes the individual women by twice using a third-person feminine singular pronoun to refer to her house and her children:

The women of my people, you drove from the house of her delights;

You removed my splendor from her children forever.

The description of the women being expelled is often interpreted as a reference to the removal of widows from their homes, but nothing in the expression itself indicates that this tragedy was limited to widows. Rather, this accusation applies to all women who had been driven from their homes. The same holds for the children. When the prophet accuses the oppressors of removing Yahweh’s splendor from her children, it seems most likely that this idea relates well to the loss of inheritance that has already been cited (2:2, 4). The loss of land meant the loss of belonging to the bodies of landowners in villages that were part of Yahweh’s inheritance, but more importantly here, it means losing the prestige of the association with belonging to Yahweh’s people, a reflection of Yahweh’s splendor. The word hādār, meaning splendor, refers to the people reflecting Yahweh’s glory. The word does not point to an inherent characteristic of Yahweh but to the umbrella of the identity associated with Yahweh’s gifting of the land.42 Hence, the metaphorical poetic imagery of 2:9 assumes by using word hādār (splendor) that Yahweh’s people reflect Yahweh’s splendor when inheriting the land, a gift that the oppressors have now taken away by their actions.

10 The announcement of punishment follows the accusations of 2:8–9. In 2:10, Yahweh commands the oppressors to leave because this is not the resting place. Two fundamentally different interpretations of the verse appear in scholarly commentaries. Some interpret at least the first part of the verse as the words of the oppressors.43 In this interpretation, the command to leave presumably continues the accusations of the crimes of the oppressors for what they have done by quoting their own words to the women and children they expelled in 2:9. Other commentators, however, treat 2:10 as the announcement of punishment, which makes better sense. Allen sees the words as a “grim parody of their orders” to the people whom they dispossessed.44 Similarly, Mays and Jeremias treat these words as the word of the prophet commanding the oppressors to vacate the lands they have taken, but these two scholars also see the verse as an early exilic appropriation because the meaning of the word resting place can be interpreted in the Deuteronomistic sense as a synonym for the promised land.45 They see the phrase resting place as corresponding to the religiously charged term for the land of promise (see Deut 12:9; 1 Kgs 8:56; and Jer 3:19).

Both interpretations make sense to a certain degree. If used as a quotation from either the oppressors or the prophet, the term resting place functions as a term for the homeland of the people. In the former case, it refers to those who have experienced forced eviction. If used as a word from the prophet to the oppressors, the command to leave makes sense because Yahweh was going to cleanse the sacred covenantal land that was given with grievous destruction. What the oppressors thought they had attained would be no more. Importantly, the continuation of punishment in 2:10b seems to interpret 2:10a as punishment, because it announces the impurity of the land using another religiously loaded term (unclean) that appears when prophets condemn Israel of idolatry (Hos 5:3; 6:10; Ezek 20:30). In this sense, Mic 2:10 also fits with the perspective of 1:5–7, an exilic condemnation of Jerusalem’s idolatry associated with the sins of Samaria. While both interpretations could make sense, the verse functions better as a verdict than as a continuation of the accusations of the previous verses, and thus is interpreted here as the words of Yahweh to the oppressors:

Arise and go for this is not the resting place.

Because it has become unclean, it will be destroyed,

And the destruction will be grievous.

The command to leave can be read against the impending attack by Sennacherib, as some have done.46 The command to leave stipulates that Yahweh’s land has been defiled. The verbs become unclean and destroyed are both feminine forms and thus presuppose resting place as the subject. The verdict also cites the problem using a perfect verb (because it has become unclean) while the punishment appears in the imperfect (it will be destroyed). This change fits the pronouncement of the verdict of what has happened and the punishment that will soon take place. The final phrase intensifies the level of destruction. It contains a masculine participle (will be grievous) because the noun destruction is masculine.

11 The final verse of the unit ends the disputation with the prophet speaking, though in part of 2:11 the prophet polemically quotes the words of a false prophet who offers to prophesy in return for payment. The sarcasm comes through loud and clear when the false prophet offers to preach, not for money, but for wine and liquor. The implications are clear. No genuine prophet would say that Yahweh would condone the actions of the oppressors, so their message can only be classified as wind and falsehood. They offer to preach for alcohol, which implies they would become drunk and would continue to prophesy to the people oppressing their countrymen. In other words, only a liar and a drunk would prophesy that the oppressors were conducting the will of Yahweh with their actions.

The syntax of the sentence offers a conditional if … then construction. One does not normally expect the word lû for if in examples of case law. One typically finds such hypothetical cases beginning with ʾim or kî to introduce the condition because it has happened. By contrast, this verse uses lû, which normally appears in conditional sentences where the speaker casts doubt on the believability of such a condition, almost as though saying, “Could you even believe that….”47 In what could almost be described as a mic-drop moment, this statement returns to challenge the prophets with which the unit began by condemning false prophets who drool their words. Micah 2:11 uses the same root (twice) that appeared in 2:6, as a charge the false prophets leveled against Micah. The word can be translated as preach or drool. The fact that the prophet accuses the false prophets as behaving improperly (walking after wind and falsehood) and of lying castigates the prophet’s abilities. The fact that the prophet quotes the false prophet claiming he is willing to sell his message (I will drool/preach for you for wine and liquor) leaves nothing to the imagination. If you believe a drunken prophet, then the drunken prophet will lead you into grievous ruin.





C. HOPE BEYOND JUDGMENT (2:12–13)


12I will utterly gather Jacob, all of you. I will completely collect the remnant of Israel. Together, I will make him like a flock in the pen,a like a herd in its meadow. They will be noisyb with people.c

13The one who breaks out goes up before them. They break out and pass through the gate and march out through it. They make their king pass by before them, and Yahweh is at their head.

a. The LXX apparently does not recognize the idiom for pen for sheep and instead translates the same consonants bṣrh as “in distress,” assuming a preposition attached to the word ṣārâ (“distress”). This noun comes from the root ṣrr that connotes distress as “constraint” rather than the less common nuance that derives from the root bṣr but means “cut off” (in the sense of grape harvesting, “be fortified,” or “inaccessible,” hence the sense of enclosure; Clines, CDCH, 53). Some (e.g., HALOT) interpret the consonants as an alternative spelling (ṣirâ) of the Arabic word ṣirat (“sheepfold,” “pen”), but this word could also be a common Semitic root.48

b. The fact that the verb is a third-person feminine plural verb is unusual. The feminine plural verb assumes the antecedent is the flock since ṣōʾn can be either feminine or masculine, but the collective idea uses the feminine plural (e.g., Gen 12:16; 30:43; Num 22:40; Jer 50:6). The noun “herd” (ʿēder) is masculine, however, and usually a combination of masculine and feminine groups takes a masculine verb.

c. Jan Wagenaar believes the consonantal text originally meant “from Edom” and should be read with 2:13 as the origin of the return from Edom.49 The reconstruction involves several points of conjecture, and arguing against this interpretation is the fact that no ancient source makes the connection between the final word of 2:12 and the opening phrase of 2:13.

Since the end of the nineteenth century, the history of critical interpretation of this short unit demonstrates the difficulty of interpreting these verses in their context. For much of this period, scholars largely treated the verses as a late salvific addition to the book of Micah, but a substantive minority has treated them as negative words pronouncing judgment rather than weal.50 Still others focus upon the distinction between all of Jacob (= Judah) and the remnant of Israel as the key to understanding.51 Many scholars treat these two verses as structurally significant for the book of Micah since the alternation of judgment and promise characterizes the book.52 Others treat the verses as a continuation of the surrounding message of impending punishment (or punishment and eventual deliverance).53 At the heart of these interpretations lies a basic question of how to interpret the ambiguous imagery of the sheep, the one who breaches the pen, and the leadership of Yahweh.

The speaker of 2:12 must be Yahweh, because the action in these verses can only be the action of Yahweh: Who else could gather Jacob and the remnant of Israel and who else could bring them together like a flock in the pen? The speaker of 2:13 requires a more complex and fluid analysis. The first part of the verse continues the description of the sheep from 2:12 without any indication of a change of speaker. The second half of the verse refers to Yahweh in the third person, which forces the interpreter to explain the change of perspective. Should the reader of these verses interpret the change as Yahweh’s speech in 2:12 giving way to the prophet, or does one envision a consistent speaker with an inconsistent style that changes from first-person divine speech to third-person references to the deity? The latter seems more likely in this context since the prophetic speech in the preceding verses has already demonstrated a style in which the prophet “speaks” the words of the opponents as well as his own words on behalf of Yahweh. This presumption of the prophet as spokesperson for the deity appears throughout prophetic literature and frequently makes it difficult to distinguish the prophet’s words from those of Yahweh.54 Hence, 2:12–13 will be treated as a single speech unit. One cannot distinguish two formal speakers, but only one speaker appears whose identity one must infer from inconsistent clues. At times, Yahweh appears to be the speaker while at other times, the speaker refers to Yahweh in the third person. More likely, we should conceptualize the prophet speaking for Yahweh, though the prophet sometimes slips back into his own voice by referring to the deity in the third person.

12 Micah 2:12 announces Yahweh’s gathering of the remnant, but the purpose of the gathering can be, and has been, interpreted variously as both a promise and a threat. The image of gathering a remnant appears elsewhere in Jer 23:3 and 40:15 in contexts that presuppose this gathering is a good thing. The problem, however, is that the verb used here (ʾsp) is different than the verb (qbṣ) used in those contexts, and ʾsp has both positive connotations (to “gather” like crops) and negative connotations (to “take away” to prison or to send into exile). Only the context determines which meaning of the verb applies, but such a decision remains complicated in 2:12–13 because the context contains both ideas. Micah 2:12 speaks about the people metaphorically as sheep while 2:13 speaks of sending the population and its king into exile.

The dominant feature of these verses concerns the extent to which the sheep metaphor controls the meaning. The verses explicitly use the metaphor of flock (ṣōʾn) in 2:12 by using two different words (flock and herd) in a parallel construction. Nevertheless, the combined entity of Jacob/Israel is referenced as one entity using the third-person masculine singular suffix (him [3ms]). Since Yahweh is the speaker and references Jacob in the third person in the opening line, one might expect a third-person pronoun on the word all, but instead one finds the second-person masculine singular suffix (2ms) attached, meaning all of you. This variation directly addresses the intended audience, thereby intensifying the speaker’s rhetorical point.

I will utterly gather Jacob, all of you [2ms].

I will completely collect the remnant of Israel.

Together, I will make him [3ms] like a flock [ṣōʾn] in the pen,

like a herd [ʿēder] in the midst of his [3ms] meadow.

They [3fp] will be noisy with people.

The fourth line above uses the word herd (ʿēder), which can refer to cows, goats, or sheep, and describes them as in the meadow. The previous line refers, however, to keeping the flock in a pen, which was common for keeping sheep in the Middle East.

The final sentence of these parallel lines describes the flock (third-person feminine plural [3fp]) that has been gathered: They will be noisy with people. The meaning of this line remains obscure. One commentator says that the line is “utterly baffling.”55 Scholars cannot agree on the root of the verb, because the form is irregular. Some scholars derive the verb from hwm (“to wander in confusion,” “rush about madly”) while others derive the verb from hmh (“to be noisy”). Most commentators (and English translations) assume that the phrase indicates the cause of the noise because of the min preposition attached to the word “human” (ʾādām) that follows the verb.56 Some see an ablative sense, suggesting the sense of “away from” instead of “because of.” The image of a noisy flock conveys the sense of size and security in the sheep metaphor. The verb translated here as to be noisy (hmh) appears elsewhere to refer to the roar of a crowd (Ps 46:7) or a city (1 Kgs 1:41; Isa 22:2), but it is fairly evenly divided between sounds in positive (1 Sam 4:5; Ruth 1:19; 1 Kgs 1:45) and negative (Pss 55:3, 17; 77:3; Deut 7:23) contexts, so this word does not easily resolve the dilemma of understanding the imagery of Mic 2:12. To make sense of the metaphor in 2:12–13, one must decide how to answer the question, Why are the people (i.e., the flock) corralled in the pen? Are they gathered as sheep for the slaughter, or does the gathering serve a different purpose?

13 The answer to this question comes in 2:13. First, one must note that in 2:12, Yahweh gathers the remnant of Israel. The presumption here is two-fold: Judgment has already occurred if there is a remnant, and the remnant has been scattered if they are now to be gathered. In addition to these suppositions, one also notes that the action of 2:13 implies they are breaking out of the pen, led by their king and Yahweh. This last statement ultimately leads one to interpret 2:12–13 as a promise. Yahweh leading the flock implies that Yahweh serves as the shepherd in the metaphor. It may not be clear where the flock is headed, but the image of Yahweh at the head certainly seems better suited for consolation than condemnation. It also should not go unnoticed that Jacob/Israel is one entity and there is one king. This promise of a single king accompanying Yahweh aligns well with promises in Hosea and Amos that many believe also represent exilic updates to the collections of those two eighth-century prophets. Specifically, Hos 1:11 (2:2) promises a restoration of the Northern and Southern Kingdoms:

The people of Judah and the people of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head; and they shall take possession of the land, for great shall be the day of Jezreel. (NRSV, emphasis added)

The promise for a single leader undoubtedly reflects a Judean perspective. Amos 9:11 provides an even more explicit statement, indicating the restoration of David’s line:

On that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen, and repair its [3fp] breaches, and raise up its [3ms] ruins, and rebuild it [3fs] as in the days of old. (NRSV)

The promise of Amos even vacillates the suffixes referring to the fallen booth in similar ways to the alternation of genders in Mic 2:12, varying between third-person feminine plural, third-person masculine singular, and third-person feminine singular. One can make sense of the changes, but they reflect a certain poetic and artistic expression.57

Why does this promise appear at the end of 2:1–11? In the context of the surrounding verses, 2:12–13 seems to presuppose a different set of enemies. In Mic 2:1–11, judgment largely focused upon inner Judean oppressors with both the power and the determination to take land from their fellow citizens. The situation probably reflects royal policies of centralization that dispossessed landowners in the highlands in order to create a system of fortifications. Yet, Mic 2:12–13 presumes that the king and Yahweh fight on the same side, and that together they will lead the remnant of Israel out of the pen in which they are held. Scholars have long suggested that 2:12–13 represents an exilic or postexilic appropriation of Micah.58 A number of scholars also associate these verses with a larger plan to structure Micah, like Hosea, as a collection of alternating messages of judgment and hope.59 This theory seems to make the most sense of the Micah collection as a whole since both of the other two major collections in Micah (4–5 and 6–7) show similar vacillations between judgment and hope.60 Yet, this promise does require the reader to change perspectives. No longer does this prophetic promise challenge the powerful landowners at the time of the eighth-century prophet. This promise jumps forward to offer a word of hope to those who have experienced trauma and displacement at the hands of an enemy. The promise announces Yahweh has not forgotten Yahweh’s promise to give the land to Jacob/Israel as an inheritance from Yahweh.

The book of Micah, like Hosea, will structure its message as a series of warnings and promises, the carrot and the stick. Yahweh expects Israel and Judah to honor the covenant obligations to which the nation committed itself. These obligations have both cultic and ethical implications. The two nations must not use Yahweh’s gifts to worship another deity (Mic 1:5–7, 9) and they must take care that they treat all of Yahweh’s people equitably within the land (2:1–11). The two kingdoms have failed to keep their side of the bargain on either front. Micah’s challenge to the powerful in chapters 1–2 leaves no doubt regarding these failures. The vacillation between oracles of judgment and deliverance puts Yahweh’s punishment into a larger context. Yahweh expects compliance from Yahweh’s people, but Yahweh has not abandoned the people. Yahweh will restore the kingdom to its place. He will lead the king and the people of Jacob/Israel to live in their land again.





1.
