The accounts of Hezekiah’s actions in Kings and Isaiah relative to Sennacherib’s attacks in 701 BCE describe the things Hezekiah did to protect Jerusalem’s water supply and only briefly allude to broader public projects he conducted. The Chronicles account goes into greater detail, adds more reference to the civil and military infrastructure credited to Hezekiah that would be consistent with the move to centralize the power of the Judean monarchy. This list is unique to the Chronicler, but presumably reflects traditions associated with Hezekiah at the time when the Chronicler adapted the material from Kings. Most date the publication of the Chronicler’s account to the latter half of the fourth century. Specifically, whereas the Kings/Isaiah parallel focuses exclusively upon those things related to the protection of Jerusalem itself after the report of Sennacherib’s conquest of the fortified cities of Judah (2 Kgs 18:13 = Isa 36:1), the Chronicler reframes the story to emphasize Hezekiah’s preparations that anticipate the threat Sennacherib posed (cf. the rephrasing of 2 Chr 32:1 + 32:2–8). In addition to protecting Jerusalem’s water supply (32:30), the Chronicler also lists new building projects (32:27–30), which the Chronicler attributes to Hezekiah’s own accumulation of wealth: building treasuries for silver and gold (32:27), storehouses for grain, wine, and oil, as well as stalls for cattle (32:28), and cities for the king (32:29). Most of these projects reflect Hezekiah’s broader aim at centralizing royal power in Jerusalem.

2. Such evidence includes the population loss in the Northern Kingdom territories as a result of Assyrian military activity (but not the complete annihilation of the land, see Knoppers, Jews and Samaritans, 42–44). At the same time, at least some of the population increase of Jerusalem involved the flight of Judean refugees in the aftermath of Assyrian incursions, including, but not limited to the former Northern Kingdom.

Joüon refers to the indirect accusative that is “indirectly subordinated to the verb” (§126a), and he notes decisively that “the indirect accusative can obviously be used with a passive verb” (§128a). Among several examples, Joüon cites Isa 45:17, which has a niphal masculine singular verb (Israel “has been saved” by Yahweh) followed by a construct chain (“salvation of perpetuity”) consisting of a feminine singular noun and a masculine plural verb: “Israel has been saved by Yahweh (with) a salvation (feminine singular) of perpetuity (masculine plural).” The nouns in the construct chain function as the indirect accusative, necessitating the addition of a preposition (“with”) in English that is not present in the Hebrew. Joüon also lists Gen 27:42, which has a hophal verb (“it was announced”), while the plural indirect object (“the words of Esau”) is preceded by the sign of the direct object (ʿet): “it was announced to Rebekah the words of Esau.” Andersen and Friedman translate the phrase in 2:6 similarly, making kəlimōt the object of the verb in English (Andersen and Freedman, 295): “He will not withdraw disgraces.” They explain their understanding as deriving from the fact that “the noun is adverbial “(causing us) shame” or “perhaps … instrumental” (Andersen and Freedman, 305–6).

Such an interpretation creates tremendous irony since most scholars understand Hezekiah’s attempts to fortify the Shephelah more strongly as an attempt to keep the Assyrians out of Jerusalem.

III. JUDGMENT ON JERUSALEM’S LEADERSHIP (3:1–12)


The third chapter of Micah consists of three subunits ending with a climactic summary verdict against Jerusalem: Micah 3:1–4 contains the prophetic response that originally continued 2:6–11; 3:5–8 offers a judgment oracle that targets false prophets; and 3:9–12 contains another judgment oracle, directed against the leaders of Jacob/Israel, whose final pronouncement (3:12) also functions as a final condemnation of Jerusalem/Zion, one whose message casts a pall over all of Mic 1–3. Both the first part (3:1–4) and last part (3:9–12) address themselves specifically to the leaders of Jacob/Israel, providing an inclusio that unites the chapter.1 Simultaneously, since the middle unit focuses its judgment against the prophets, and the final unit also includes statements against the priests along with the prophets (3:11) and the leaders (3:9; cf. 3:1), this inclusio helps define the identity of those creating the problem in Mic 3 as including both political and religious leadership.2 The message of judgment has a powerful effect not only with those reading the book of Micah by itself, but also with the reading of the Twelve as a whole and those reading the entire prophetic corpus. The Masoretic tradition marks 3:12 as the midpoint of the Book of the Twelve, providing evidence that the Twelve were copied as a single scroll. Relatedly, in the prophetic narratives of Jeremiah, the supporters of the prophet cite Mic 3:12 (see Jer 26:18) as authoritative evidence for why Jeremiah should not be put to death.





A. JUSTICE FOR LEADERS DEVOURING THEIR OWN (3:1–4)


1And Ia said,

Listen, leaders of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel.

Should you not know justice?

2Those hating good and loving evil,b

those tearing their own skinc and their flesh from their bones,

3And who devour the flesh of my people,

and strip their skin, and break their bones,

and then chop (them) in pieces just as for a pot or like flesh in the midst of a kettle.

4Then, they cry out to Yahweh,

but he does not respond to them.

Rather, he hides his face from them in that time since they have brought evil upon themselves.

a. The LXX reads “and he said,” which means the translator either had a text with wayyōʾmer rather than MT’s wāʾōmar, or the translator deliberately altered the opening for the context. Since Mur 88 also confirms the MT, the MT is followed here. Further, the prophetic speaker makes better sense of 3:1–4, which speaks of Yahweh in the third person.

b. The MT has the consonants for the noun rāʿâ (“an evil thing”), but the Masoretes indicate that the qere reading should be the adjective evil in pausal form (rāʿ). The adjective better parallels the adjective good in the first part of the verse, but the addition of a he is more difficult to explain than the loss of a he. The lacuna in Mur 88 does not allow one to confirm MT at this point. The meaning is not significantly affected in either case.

c. The phrase (those tearing their own skin) is awkward. Literally, it reads “those tearing their skin from upon themselves.” BHS and BHK suggest omitting or emending and moving the phrase. BHS suggests making the participle an imperfect by adding a yod to the front and exchanging the yod on the end to a shureq, hence yigzəlû (“they tore their skin from themselves”), but this seems unlikely based upon the plural participle form in LXX.

In the final form of the book, Mic 3:1–4 follows 2:12–13, which announces a promise of Yahweh’s ultimate deliverance that was added to the collection of Micah’s sayings in the aftermath of Jerusalem’s destruction, but the opening word of 3:1 (wāʾōmar, meaning and I said) makes far less sense as a response to the promise than it does as the continuation of the disputation in 2:6–11. The end of 2:6–11 quoted the false prophets and the I speaking in 3:1 introduces the prophet’s own response to them.3 Micah 2 likely reflects prophetic reaction to forced relocation policies that were part of a political and military move to centralize power and create more robust defensive fortifications in the Shephelah. Micah 3:1–4 pronounces a judgment oracle on the leaders of Jacob/Israel, which fits well as a continuation of this theme.4

1 The logical flow of the first unit, 3:1–4, begins with a rhetorical question from the prophet addressed to the leaders of Jacob/Israel: Should you not know justice? The accusatory nature of this question at the end of 3:1 becomes clear as the next two verses continue with a series of appositional clauses describing the action of the leaders using the extended metaphor of the butchering, flailing, and cooking of an animal to describe the brutality of the leaders toward their own people. Only with 3:4 does the irony of the rhetorical question in 3:1 come fully into focus. The Hebrew word translated justice (mišpāṭ), like the word “justice” in English, has both a positive and a negative connotation.5 Positively, justice is an ideal that requires actions that are pleasing to Yahweh and in accordance with divine order. Negatively, justice represents the action taken by Yahweh or his representatives to bring this order back into line when it has been transgressed. Thus, the rhetorical question (Should you not know justice?) could be taken one of two ways, either as an accusation of wrongdoing or as the words of a judge determining whether a plaintiff has been wronged. The descriptions in 3:2–3 allow the reader to determine quickly that this question begins an accusation, but the description of the verdict in 3:4 causes one to realize that it is the leaders themselves who have petitioned Yahweh for justice without realizing that it is their own crimes that are now creating a scenario where justice means punishing those leaders.

The call specifies the leaders of Jacob and the rulers of the house of Israel. The first term for leader (rōʾš) literally means head, and it suggests those at the top of a hierarchical structure. Nevertheless, the term as used here appears to be intended in a broader capacity. The second term, translated ruler (qāṣîn), comes from the Hebrew root qṣh II (“to decide, decree”), and thus it implies those making decisions that affect others. This term could apply to a military commander (Josh 10:24; Judg 11:11), a dictator (Isa 3:6–7), or any person in authority (see Isa 22:3).

2–3 Micah 3:2–3 consist of a series of seven appositional clauses that characterize the leaders mentioned in 3:1. The first two appositional clauses summarize the charges against the leaders as those hating good and loving evil. This statement functions on two levels—that of the immediate context and that of the broader literary context—so that the question carries considerable import. In the immediate context, this first appositional clause links what follows in 3:2–3 to the introductory question of 3:1. The clauses describe the leaders in 3:1 in philosophical terms as those who have inverted the order established by Yahweh. One should hate evil, not good; and one should love good, not evil. These two clauses represent the only ones in the unit that do not rely directly upon the metaphor of butchering and devouring an animal, but these clauses lay the foundation of the accusation proper in this oracle because they state pointedly that the leaders of 3:1 have acted contrary to the divine order. In so doing, this first appositional clause already begins to lay a foundation for answering the rhetorical question of 3:1. If, indeed, the established order has been transgressed, then in biblical terms, Yahweh must take action to restore that order.

In the extended context of the Book of the Four, the prophetic collections of Hosea and Amos have also condemned the actions of those who hate good and love evil.6 Specifically, Mic 3:1 recalls the confrontation of Amos 5:14–15, which commands the remnant of Joseph to “seek good and not evil” immediately after Amos 5:13 refers to the present as an “evil time.” Hence, 5:14–15 calls for the people of Israel to change their behavior, but by the end of Amos it has become clear that they will not. Micah continues these ideas but transfers the accusations to Judah rather than Israel alone. At several points in Mic 1–3, the prophet notes that the sins of the Northern Kingdom have reached Jerusalem (see Mic 1:5–7, 9, 12), since Judah is full of those doing evil (2:1), and in Mic 2:3, Judah has created an evil time just like Amos 5:13. The attentive reader of the larger context senses this parallel and intuits the dire warning that the accusation communicates.7

The accusations take an even more negative turn beginning with the third appositional clause, which utilizes images of slaughtering and butchering of animals as a metaphor for the actions of the leaders. And yet, this metaphor functions in two different ways whose importance should not be missed.8 The first function of the metaphor appears in Mic 3:2b, which essentially accuses the leaders of mutilating their own bodies. Implied in this metaphor is an admonition that their actions—the tearing of their own skin from their bones—creates an abhorrent picture of mutilation that can only lead to deformity and death. Yet, when one remembers that the actions of the leaders have been described in the previous chapter as actions taken against their own people in the form of forced displacement and the co-opting of land, this image functions as a grotesque accusation that the leaders do not even realize that their own actions will come back to haunt them because they themselves have begun to destroy the body, that is, the people of Yahweh.

The second function of the butcher imagery takes a more direct approach in terms of metaphorical language used to condemn the leaders. The remaining four statements of 3:3 continue to describe the leaders mentioned in 3:1 in accusatory language that focuses the analogy differently so that 3:3 moves from describing the leaders’ self-mutilation (3:2b) to equating their actions with cannibalism. The parallel lines in 3:3 begin with a summary statement that describes the leaders as [those] who devour the flesh of my people, while the remainder of the verse graphically describes the cooking process. The animal is skinned, and then its bones are broken before it is chopped into pieces and thrown into the kettle. The images are provocative and polemical. They intentionally describe the abhorrent and brutal actions of the leaders in order to underscore the scale of violence by which those actions should be interpreted. It would be hard to imagine a more powerful way to describe the callousness and coarseness of the leaders’ behavior.

4 The extended list of appositional clauses that function as accusations against the leaders (3:2–3), while powerfully provocative, does not represent the rhetorical climax of the unit, which actually appears in 3:4. After presenting this extensive and brutal list of charges against the leaders, the prophet emphatically reports their subsequent act: then [ʾaz] they cry out to Yahweh. The sarcasm of this line can hardly be overestimated: They call to Yahweh, but Yahweh does not respond to them. After utilizing the vicious, brutal, and cannibalistic images to portray their actions, the audacity of their petition to Yahweh adds to the characterization of these leaders as selfish and oblivious. Instead, Yahweh actively ignores them at the point in time when they make their petition. According to Yahweh, these leaders have brought evil upon themselves. The rhetorical logic of 3:1–4 first calls out the leaders (3:1) and then exposes their actions as self-inflicted wounds (3:2) that have created gruesome consequences (3:3). Nevertheless, 3:4 begins by announcing that these very leaders cry out for help to Yahweh when the consequences of these deeds begin to dawn on them. The remainder of 3:4 disabuses them of any hope that Yahweh will act on their behalf. Yahweh ignores their plea (he hides his face from them) because their actions have consequences. They have created their own calamity.





B. JUSTICE FOR FALSE PROPHETS: THEY WILL NOT SPEAK (3:5–8)


5Thus says Yahweh against the prophets who lead my people astray,

To those having something to eat,a they cry out peace.

But whoever does not give them something for their mouth,

they consecrate war against him.

6Therefore, it will be night for you, without vision,

and it will become darkb for you, without divination.

And the sun will set upon the prophets,

and the day will turn dark over them.

7And those seeing visions will be ashamed,

and those divining will be abashed.

All of them will cover their mustache,

because there is no response from God.

8On the other hand, I am filled with strength,

with the spirit of Yahweh, and justice, and might,

to declare to Jacob his rebellion and to Israel his sin.

a. Literally, MT reads “those biting with their teeth,” but—following several English translations—the subject of this idiom refers to the prophets who lead my people astray. Concurrently, this line contrasts with the line that follows, which clearly refers to those who do not give something to the prophets. Consequently, the idiom must refer to those having food and giving it to the prophets (in contrast to those who do not pay the prophets with food).

b. The LXX renders the phrase from the Hebrew using the feminine noun skotia while the Nahal Hever manuscript (8Ḥev 1) uses a verbal form of the root (skotasthēsetai) that translates as become dark. The different Greek phrases do not change the meaning and do not reflect a text that differs from MT. It represents two distinct attempts to put the Hebrew into Greek. The Nahal Hever manuscript is dated to the first century CE and is thus later than the LXX.

Whereas the previous unit condemned the action of the leaders, 3:5–8 turns its attention to false prophets, those who knowingly offer words of promise (instead of judgment) so long as they receive payment for their troubles.9 The structure of 3:5–8 follows the typical pattern of a judgment oracle: It begins with a messenger formula (Thus says Yahweh) followed by a statement identifying the object of judgment—and simultaneously describing the crimes for which they are judged (3:5)—before turning to an extended pronouncement of the verdict (3:6–8), whose transition appears in the typical marker therefore that begins 3:6. This transparent structure gives the unit the feel of a self-standing unit that has been positioned here for rhetorical effect, yet its integration with the themes and wording of the surrounding units causes many recent commentators to treat chapter 3:1–12 as a single composition with three parts.10 The condemnation of prophets in 3:5–8 follows the judgment oracle against the leaders in 3:1–4, thus broadening the condemnation of behavior into the religious realm. In the middle of the next portion, 3:11 adds priests and prophets to the list of leaders, thereby specifying which political and religious functionaries are accused of accepting money to influence the performance of their duties.11 In short, then, Mic 3 cumulatively accuses the entire gamut of religious and political leadership of Judah for leading the people astray in order to better their own economic situation.12

5 Micah 3:5 begins with a classic introduction of a judgment oracle in the form of a messenger formula: Thus says Yahweh. This formula identifies the speaker as the prophet who immediately identifies the prophets as the recipient of judgment followed by a series of three accusations. The first accusation functions as a general summation of the wrongdoings of the prophets in the form of a participial clause: the prophets who lead my people astray. The next two clauses in this verse describe their misdeeds from two sides, essentially accusing them of disobedience and greed. The first of these two lines accuses them of proclaiming peace (šālôm), but the context and the preceding phrase force the reader to infer that this message of peace was not the message Yahweh would have them deliver. Those prophets who are proclaiming peace are also described as “biting their teeth,” a phrase that portrays them as withholding the words they should really be speaking. The next phrase continues the condemnation by describing their actions as motivated by greed: whoever does not give them something for their mouth. Simultaneously, this last phrase builds off the images of the preceding accusation in order to amplify the charges. While the second line accuses these prophets of proclaiming peace, the third line indicts them for doing the opposite (consecrating war). These prophets take on anyone who does not remunerate them for their prophecies. The prophet satirically refers to the payments as something for their mouth. Combined, these two lines condemn prophets who make pronouncements of weal for those willing to pay while speaking judgment against those unwilling or unable to pay.

6 Micah 3:6 begins with therefore, a term typically used to mark the change from accusation to the verdict in judgment oracles.13 The verdict, expressed in 3:6–7 is the removal of Yahweh’s communication with the false prophets. They will no longer receive a vision, nor will they be able to provide a divination about the future. Instead, they will find themselves in darkness as expressed in two parallel lines. These prophets who make their living pronouncing prophecies will be cut off from Yahweh. The sun will set on these prophets while the day will turn dark. They will not see (or hear) anything from Yahweh. The verdict leads rhetorically to an unusual element in 3:8, where the prophet delivering the judgment oracle contrasts his own continuing power with the impotence of the false prophets. In this sense, the prophetic I in 3:8 ties back to the I of 3:1 and continues the political confrontation that began in chapter 2.

The verdict in 3:6–7 contains two pairs of parallel versets in which the first set (3:6) describes the judgment against the prophets while the second set (3:7) describes their reaction to that judgment. The judgment proper in 3:6 plays with images of darkness and light in order to make the point that the false prophets will lose their ability to communicate with Yahweh.

Therefore, it will be night for you, without vision;

and it will become dark for you, without divination.

And the sun will set upon the prophets,

and the day will turn dark over them.

Each of these parallel lines announces judgment in relationship to darkness and the lack of light. The first two statements announce judgment as darkness, but each line further classifies this darkness as the loss of the prophets’ ability to communicate. This loss is described in terms that offer specific judgment against prophets: they will be without vision and without divination. They will be without their means of communication with the deity. They will be left alone, isolated in darkness. The third and fourth versets reverse the comparison by focusing upon the elements of light (the sun and the day) that will no longer provide light. The sun will set, and daylight turns to darkness for them. These four lines are closely intertwined by these images of light and dark used to isolate the prophets who have challenged Micah.

7 Micah 3:7 focuses upon the consequences of the judgment announced in 3:6 by describing the reaction of the prophets as shame and silence. The four versets of 3:6 are balanced by four versets in 3:7.

And those seeing visions will be ashamed,

and those divining will be abased.

All of them will cover their mustache,

because there is no response from God.

The first two of these versets both form a line of classic synonymous parallelism and reach back to the first pair of statements from 3:6 in which the prophets were punished so that they were without vision (noun from the root ḥzh) and divination (infinitival noun from the root qsm). In 3:7, those punished are described with participles using the same verbs (ḥzh and qsm). Yet, the focus of 3:7 centers not upon what will happen to them (the inability to communicate with Yahweh), but upon the consequences of their inability to communicate with Yahweh. They will be ashamed and abashed.

The second half of 3:7 describes an action that presupposes the shame of 3:7a. When the prophet declares that all of them will cover their mustaches, the prophet is also describing an act of abasement.14 By putting their hands over their mouths (i.e., covering their mustaches) these prophets graphically acknowledge the consequences of their punishment. Without visions and without the power to perform divination, the prophets have nothing to say. By covering their mouths, they acknowledge the futility of speaking. A prophet who cannot communicate with the deity has no message, and the last statement of 3:7 drives home that point: God has ceased to respond to these “prophets.”

8 The unit concludes in 3:8 with a statement of contrast in which the genuine prophetic character (Micah) contrasts his own power under the spirit of Yahweh with the impotence of the other prophets.15 This verse begins with a strong adversative (ʾûlām) followed immediately by the first-person subject pronoun I that signals the contrast (On the other hand, I). Micah maintains he is filled with strength, justice, and might that come from the spirit of Yahweh. The abundance of the prophet’s strength (kōaḥ) stands in stark contrast to the impotence of the false prophets, and even the syntactical structure conveys that sense. A single verb, I am filled with, receives not one but four different objects (strength, the spirit of Yahweh, justice, and might). Together, this list conveys a sense of authority and alignment with Yahweh that offers a direct contrast with the false prophets whom the prophet confronts in 3:5–7. The spirit of Yahweh fills this prophet,16 which affirms that the judgment of 3:6–7 has not affected this speaker’s prophetic role since the spirit of Yahweh is often associated with genuine prophetic activity.17 The claim that he is also filled with justice (mišpāṭ) implies that, again contrary to the false prophets, this prophet is closely aligned with the order expected by Yahweh.18 On either side of these two claims, the words strength and might solidify the impression of power that belongs to the prophet of Yahweh. This contrasting description of power leads to a purpose, namely, to contrast Micah’s character with that of the false prophets. The false prophets do not respond to Micah’s critique, while this prophet of Yahweh conveys an image of power whose express purpose is to speak for Yahweh. He will declare to Jacob/Israel that it has done wrong. This purpose statement uses two different words for sin. The first one (pešaʿ), often translated as rebellion, emphasizes a state of willful disobedience, while the second word, usually translated simply as sin (ḥaṭṭʾāt), carries the sense of falling short.19 This purpose statement picks up the motifs from 1:5 (rebellion, sin, Israel, and Jacob), and this inclusio prepares the reader for the final unit of the early collection of Micah sayings in 3:9–12.





C. LEADERSHIP CAUSES JERUSALEM’S DESTRUCTION (3:9–12)


9Hear this, heads of the house of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel,

those treating justice as an abomination,

and who twist everything that is upright.

10The onesa building Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with injustice,

11Her leaders judge for a bribe,

and priests instruct for a price,

and her prophets divine for money.

They lean upon Yahweh, saying,

“Is Yahweh not in our midst? Evil will not come upon us.”

12Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field,

and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble,

and the mountain of the house will become a high place in the forest.

a. MT has a singular participle (bōneh) while the Greek has a masculine plural participle (bdelussomenoi). The difference is only one letter when retroverted back into unpointed Hebrew (bnh in the MT compared to bny in the Hebrew text reflected in the Greek). Whether or not the Greek text was original, the sense is clearly the same. See the commentary below.

9 The climactic unit of Mic 1–3 takes the form of a judgment oracle against Judah.20 The next section (9b–11) functions as the accusation against the various leaders of Jerusalem (administrators, priests, and prophets). Finally, 3:12 announces the verdict: Yahweh will completely destroy Jerusalem for the sins of its leaders.

The last unit of chapter 3 begins with a call to attention (3:9a) using a plural imperative (hear) along with the feminine singular pronoun this (zōʾt) as the direct object. This demonstrative pronoun often refers to that which follows, as is the case here. The accusation that follows (9b–11) specifies those holding a range of civic and cultic positions more concretely (it probably refers to any kind of magistrate, as well as the specific mention of priests and prophets). The common denominator in their behavior stems from their use of their positions to enhance their own wealth. The invocation of the leaders creates an inclusio to the beginning of the speech on Mic 3:1–12.

The combination of the house of Jacob and the house of Israel in 3:9a has appeared previously in Micah (see 3:1 and the use of Jacob/Israel in 1:5–7), but the precise meaning of these terms remains ambiguous. They can refer to leaders of the two kingdoms, Judah and Israel; they can be interpreted as synonyms (in which case, they would refer to Judah since Jerusalem is the explicit focus of the oracle according to 3:12); or they could refer to the land as it was conceptualized in the time of David and Solomon (the territory of a unified Israel before Jeroboam I broke away from Solomon’s son Rehoboam, taking ten of the twelve tribes with him [2 Kgs 12]). The remainder of 3:9, however, continues with two clauses that list accusations of ethical violations (making justice an abomination and making crooked that which is upright).21 The accusations assume that the problems are ongoing, so it is doubtful that the term house of Israel refers to the Northern Kingdom since Samaria was destroyed in 722 and most scholars believe this passage refers to the time leading up to the siege of Sennacherib in 701. There is not, however, agreement on how closely the oracle is associated with those events.22 The rulers of the the Northern Kingdom would have been taken away nearly twenty years earlier. Both terms justice and upright have legal and cultic implications that refer to proper action within the community as commanded ultimately by God.23 The accusations of Mic 3:9b–11, however, invert these expectations because the leaders are not, in the words of the prophet, performing their roles as leaders properly. They do more than just ignore Yahweh’s expectations since they knowingly make decisions based on their own benefit, not what is right. They treat justice as something to be sold to the highest bidder. The verb tʿb is a verbal form of the noun meaning abomination, used to describe that which is abhorrent to Yahweh. Used with justice as the direct object, the verb conveys a strong sense of condemnation for those perverting right and wrong. The adjective upright (yāšār) in the next clause conveys the sense of straight and proper while the verb used with it (ʿqš) means “to twist” or “make crooked.” These two lines start to make specific (albeit still broad) accusations implying that the leaders of the country have perverted Yahweh’s intentions for the people.

10 The accusation in 3:10 turns from the broader political terms (the house of Jacob and the house of Israel) to the more geographically specific terms Zion and Jerusalem. The accusations of wrongdoing also become more intense (building … with bloodshed, … with injustice) than the previous verse. In other words, the prophet accuses these leaders of using violence to enforce their unjust decisions. On the one hand, the mention of those24 building Jerusalem and Zion with bloodshed seems to imply both that some group in the city is being condemned and that the size of Jerusalem grew significantly in the late eighth century.25 On the other hand, if one considers Mic 2, then these problems were not isolated to Jerusalem. The contextual logic of this condemnation suggests that the events condemned in 3:10 are the same as those in chapter 2 that condemn the king’s policies of taking land owned by someone else and using it to fortify the country in a way that makes it harder for armies to reach Jerusalem. Hezekiah had designs for centralizing the monarchy.26 Zion was being expanded, and land was being confiscated to defend the king in Jerusalem from invaders. By calling out the leaders of the house of Jacob/Israel (3:9) who build Zion with bloodshed and injustice (3:10), the prophet likely intends those who were implementing Hezekiah’s policies. They are not, however, the only ones whom the prophet condemns, since 3:11 will delineate a more specific set of religious and political leaders.27 In essence, 3:9–10 focus upon those whom the prophet addressed more directly in 3:1–4 while 3:11 takes on the cultic leadership as well (more like 3:5–8). In this sense 3:9–11 performs a summary role before the climactic verse of 3:12 announces Yahweh’s verdict to destroy Jerusalem.

Scholarship on this text treats the parallel terms Zion and Jerusalem variously. The majority of commentators see the terms as virtual synonyms and often do not even comment upon the pairing.28 Others distinguish the terms as referring to the city at large (Jerusalem) and the temple area (Zion).29 Additionally, the reference to Zion could evoke “Lady Zion” or “Daughter Zion” in anticipation of Lady Zion’s appearance in Mic 4:8, 10, 11, 13, 14 (cf. also 7:8–10). She functions as the personification of Jerusalem and the consort of Yahweh in a number of prophetic texts.30

The specific condemnations are phrased in a way that requires one to consider the literary horizon of 3:10. A number of commentators have suggested that Mic 3:1–4, 9–12 contains specific citations by and allusions to other prophetic and biblical texts:31

Micah 3:1 draws upon Hos 5:1aβ.

Micah 3:2 picks up Amos 5:15 (which, like Mic 3, is part of a text whose Leitwort is mišpāṭ).

Micah 3:10 and Hab 2:12 refer to Jerusalem using virtually identical phrases: Those building Zion/“a city with bloodshed” respectively.

Micah 3:11 draws upon Amos 5:14–15.

Micah 3:12 is the source of an explicit citation in Jer 26:18.32

These intertextual relationships are not all cut from the same cloth. In three instances (Mic 3:1, 2, 11) Micah appears to be the borrowing text. Specifically, texts in Mic 3 draw upon texts that were part of an early collection that connects three of the writings of the Book of the Four.33 By contrast, a later text (Jer 26:18) explicitly cites Mic 3:12. It is difficult to classify with certainty in which direction, if either, the borrowing of the final parallel (Mic 3:10 = Hab 2:12) occurs. The phrase (Zion/a city built by bloodshed) could be an idiom used to castigate a group harming a city.34 Most commentators assume that 3:10 (as part of 3:9–12) would have been composed prior to the time of Habakkuk. Both texts function intricately within their contexts, and the dates of the Habakkuk material could be contemporary with Jeremiah or considerably later.

11 In Mic 3:11, the accusatory language of 3:10 becomes more concrete and more specific, both in terms of singling out specific groups (leaders, priests, and prophets) and in terms of naming specific actions (officials taking bribes, priests and prophets charging money for teaching). Micah 3:11 builds upon and presupposes 3:10 since the antecedent of the third-person feminine singular pronoun her presumes the city of Jerusalem (and Zion) mentioned in 3:10. The word translated as her leaders (rōʾš) literally means “heads” and is the same word used in 3:9 to indict the leaders of the house of Jacob/Israel. The two verses refer to the same group, specifically the leadership circles in Jerusalem, who claim responsibility for and exercise power over the state and the city. While 3:9 classifies the nature of the crimes with ethical and theological terms, 3:11 lists three specific groups of this political and religious leadership that have violated the expectations of Yahweh because of their own greed and the misperception of their own role in Yahweh’s kingdom. First, the prophet accuses the leaders of behavior that is motivated by greed. All three groups are indicted for doing their jobs, but more specifically for the way they do their jobs. They charge money for fulfilling the responsibilities of their positions. The immediate context must be kept in mind to understand the specific nature of these charges. The prophet does not condemn these groups for earning a living. Rather, in this context, the prophet castigates this group for ignoring justice (3:9) and twisting what is right and proper (3:9). Consequently, when 3:11 says that her leaders judge for a bribe, it means that money influences the decision; when it says that the priests instruct for a price or that her prophets divine for money, it refers to special treatment for those willing and able to pay. The leaders adjudicate by weighing out the money they receive rather than by weighing the merits of the case. The priests offer instruction for hire without counting the cost of serving only those who can afford to pay. And the prophets concern themselves only with profits when they work for silver.

Second, the leadership appears to be oblivious to the way in which their behavior harms the community. These groups justifiy their own actions and their own positions with a theological statement that presupposes a circular logic often used by those in power. The introduction to their quoted speech is telling: They lean upon Yahweh, saying. This introduction would, in other contexts, read like a pious statement honoring those whom it describes as adherents of the deity, but in this context, it reeks of sarcasm. The antecedent of the pronoun they can only refer to the leaders, priests, and prophets who are abusing their roles in the community. Further, this introduction and the quotation that follows function rhetorically within the accusation of the judgment oracle and thus refer to behavior that the prophet is condemning. The content of their quotation becomes even more telling. They ask, Is Yahweh not in our midst? This question presupposes both a positive retort and a broader theological framework. How would one know that Yahweh is in our midst? One would infer Yahweh’s presence by the well-being of the temple, the city, and the political structure. If the temple and the city are safe and the king is on the throne, then in the ancient world, the assumption would be that the deity was present and satisfied. If Yahweh is present, then one must assume that evil will not come upon the land. Their statement implies Yahweh’s silence equals Yahweh’s presence and Yahweh’s tacit approval. For the prophet, however, their claim that evil will not come demonstrates the utter incompetence of the leaders to perceive that the true danger derives from their actions. In short, the claim climaxes the accusations of 3:9–12 while also summarizing much of the accusatory tone of Mic 2–3. Simultaneously, this speech provides the turning point where the judgment oracle of 3:9–12 turns from accusation to verdict in 3:12.

12 Micah 3:12 plays an important role in at least three ways: First, 3:12 functions significantly in the immediate context of 3:9–12; second, it serves as the culmination of judgment in Mic 1–3; and finally, it plays a role in the broader canonical context of the Book of the Twelve and the Prophets. In the immediate context, Mic 3:12 signals the shift from accusation to verdict in the oracle of 3:9–12, one that pronounces judgment against the leaders of Zion/Jerusalem. The term therefore signals the shift to the verdict of the judgment oracle, and the antecedent of the second-person masculine plural pronoun you must be interpreted as the leaders mentioned in 3:9, 11 (heads of the house of Jacob/Israel, including the priests and prophets). Simultaneously, the parallel mention of Zion/Jerusalem picks up the city as mentioned in 3:10. The judgment oracle that condemns the greed of the religious and political leaders of Judah pronounces destruction that will result in Jerusalem’s destruction.

Three parallel statements portray a sequence of images that build off of one another to portray the coming devastation. First, the city will be plowed like a field. This image conveys the upheaval of a plowshare turning over the soil, but the analogy depicts Jerusalem’s destruction not the planting of grain. What will be overturned is not dirt and weeds but buildings and lives. The second statement describes the consequence of this plowing: Jerusalem will become a heap of ruins. As an extension of the plow metaphor in the first line, this line portrays the city as having been physically ripped apart so that the city’s buildings lie in mounds of stone and dirt. The third statement indicates the long-term nature of the overthrow. Jerusalem will become overgrown by neglect, meaning it will not be rebuilt in the short term: the temple mountain will be unrecognizable as a temple. It will only look like a mound of vegetation in the forest.

This pronouncement of Jerusalem’s destruction must have been memorable. Given that most Micah scholarship suggests that 3:9–12 reflects the early core of the book and was transmitted orally, if not in written form, from the time of the prophet from Moresheth, then one can see why this oracle appears at the end of the early collection. The prophet warns the country’s leadership that Jerusalem will not survive if it chooses to continue its path. This oracle presumes a situation at the end of the eighth century BCE when Hezekiah attempted to build a series of fortifications in order to keep the Assyrians from taking Judean territory, but more specifically to stop them from reaching Jerusalem.

In addition to the immediate context, scholars usually treat this verse as the culmination of the early collection of Mic 1–3. Micah 3:12 uses the language of Mic 1:6 (heap of rubble, field), thus creating an inclusio between the end of chapter 3 and the opening rhetorical unit of 1:2–7. The inclusio deliberately draws a parallel between Yahweh’s destruction of Samaria in 1:6 and the pronouncement of Jerusalem’s destruction in 3:12. This language raises two questions: Is the link intentional and, if so, which direction of borrowing best explains the link? At least three observations suggest that the compiler of chapters 1–3 intentionally created the link. First, the word ruins is rare. It occurs only five times in the Hebrew Bible (Job 30:24; Ps 79:1; Jer 26:18; Mic 1:6; 3:12), with three of those five (Ps 79:1; Jer 26:18; Mic 3:12) occurring in the plural as explicit references to the destruction of Jerusalem. Second, only three of these references occur in prophetic texts, and all three relate to Micah. Beyond the specific occurrence of this word in Mic 1:6 and 3:12, Jer 26:18 represents an explicit quote of Mic 3:12. Third, the statement that Jerusalem will become a heap of ruins fits perfectly well within the judgment oracle of 3:9–12, while 1:6 uses the same word (albeit in the singular) with reference to Samaria. This hermeneutic plays a strong role in the redactional material from the exilic period that has been imposed upon an early collection of Micah’s sayings.35 This final point also provides the key for understanding how the link between 1:6 and 3:12 originated. Micah 1:2–7 shows signs that it has been composed (or so heavily redacted that one can no longer distinguish a clear foundational layer) with an eye toward other texts. These verses not only evidence a literary horizon within the Book of the Four, but also provide a text that exhibits the same theological presuppositions as 2 Kgs 17. Namely, 2 Kgs 17 and Mic 1:2–7 interpret the destruction of Samaria as a warning to Jerusalem. Consequently, Mic 1:6 appropriates the judgment saying from 3:12 but applies it to Samaria to create the parallel between Samaria and Jerusalem. By the time that the reader comes to 3:12, the reader has encountered numerous reasons for Jerusalem’s destruction.

Beyond its function as the culmination of chapters 1–3, Mic 3:12 also plays a noteworthy role in the Book of the Twelve and in the Jeremiah tradition. Within the Book of the Twelve, the Masoretes marked this verse as the center point of the Book of the Twelve. The marginal notes of Codex Leningrad specify 3:12 as “The midpoint of the scroll.” Since 3:12 is not the middle of Micah but does comport perfectly with the Masoretic note at the end of Malachi, clearly one must interpret the scroll to which this note refers as the Book of the Twelve.36

Also, within the larger prophetic canon, the verse plays a distinctive and unique role because the trial of Jeremiah explicitly quotes it as supporting evidence for why Jeremiah should not be put to death for treason. Jeremiah 26 represents a prophetic narrative recounting how Jeremiah’s predicting of Jerusalem’s destruction led to his arrest and trial for treason.37 Those coming to his defense (the elders of the land) essentially cite Mic 3:12 (in Jer 26:18) as a legal precedent. Nearly a century earlier than Jeremiah, they argue, Micah predicted Jerusalem’s destruction, but King Hezekiah did not kill Micah. Jeremiah 26:19 explains why Micah’s prophecy did not come true in his own lifetime: because Hezekiah did not put Micah to death but instead responded by entreating Yahweh to change his mind, which saved Jerusalem. Hence the Jeremiah tradition not only knows Mic 3:12 but credits this speech as the reason for Jerusalem’s deliverance from Assyria at the end of the eighth century BCE in the reign of Hezekiah. This hermeneutic sheds considerable light on how those in the late seventh/early sixth century understood the text of Mic 1–3 as a prophecy to be read in light of the Assyrian crisis leading to the siege of Sennacherib. This hermeneutic will continue in the growth of the Micah corpus itself, as will be evident with the interpretations of the later additions of Mic 4–5 and 6–7 in this commentary. One suspects, given the importance of 3:12 for the larger prophetic canon, that its position in the exact middle of the Twelve may not be accidental, but the process would be nearly impossible to conceptualize and describe.38

Those who read Mic 3 as part of Christian scripture would do well to recognize how central its message is to the way that Jesus approached his own ministry and the way we should conduct our own lives. Micah portrays the prophet as one who is unafraid to challenge the political and religious leaders of his day. On one level, this might not strike us as all that odd since American politicians are critiqued all the time. The United States has a history of protected speech that is part of our democratic ideal embedded into the constitution of our country in the first amendment (also called the Bill of Rights). That amendment reads:

Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.

This amendment denies congress the power of establishing religion or prohibiting people from practicing their own religion. Those explicit limitations are powerful roadblocks that have stood the test of time, though numerous court cases have also been filed to determine what constitutes a religion or what happens if someone’s religion has practices that are illegal.

But our system of government is a republic, where political leaders are elected to fill certain roles for a specific number of years. The enactment of any law must be passed by two separate houses of congress and signed by the head of the administrative branch (president or governor) who is also elected for a specific time period.

These rules did not apply in Judah in the eighth century BCE (as was the case throughout the ancient Near East). There were no elections. The ruler of Judah was a king who did not have to pass laws through congress. He could simply declare something by fiat. There was no such thing as protected speech. If someone spoke against the king, the king could execute that person on the spot (see Jer 26:20–23). And yet, the Bible contains numerous stories of those whom Yahweh expects to challenge the king. Samuel condemns Saul (1 Sam 15); Nathan confronts David for killing Uriah by using a parable (2 Sam 12); Amos challenges Jeroboam (Amos 7:9–17). Isaiah confronts Hezekiah (2 Kgs 20:13–19). In short, the Bible shows how Yahweh uses prophets to confront kings.

Micah speaks truth to power, not in ideological rants as one often sees on social media in our day. We tend to rant against those who are not part of our chosen tribe (especially political parties or those who disagree with us on certain social issues). Micah does not side with the powerful. Micah sees how political leaders, priests, and prophets use their social status to line their own pockets. He calls out judges who take bribes to decide cases. He calls out priests who instruct only those who can pay and prophets who tell those who pay what they want to hear and claim it is a message from God.

When we read Mic 3, with whom do we identify? Likely, most of us probably think of ourselves in the role of the prophet. We want to think we would stand up to those who were creating injustice. We want to think we would distinguish right from wrong and do what is right. Yet, the prophet in Mic 3 is called to declare to Yahweh’s people how they have rebelled against Yahweh and how they have fallen short. History is littered with cases where Christian communities have done the same. The history of slavery in this country lasted so long, in part, because the church (especially in the South) sided with the wealthy landowners rather than slaves. When the South lost the Civil War, politicians found ways to take away the right to vote from persons of color, and the church largely remained silent. When immigrants came in waves in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, bigots sought ways to isolate them and keep them down. Sometimes, Protestant churches stood by because the immigrants came from Catholic countries. Sometimes, the church stood by because the nationalities of the immigrants came from Asia. When the civil rights movement began to take hold in Black churches in the 1950s and 1960s, white denominations largely remained silent.

Christian churches today and their members need to hear the words of Micah as though they are directed to them. The prophetic books were compiled for the believing community not so they could rejoice over judgment heaped upon others. Rather, the prophetic message challenges us not to become complacent. Do we speak “religious truth” because we benefit from the claims we make? Or, do we ask whether our behavior and ideas serve our own interests rather than the role of justice? Yahweh typically stands on the side of those who are wronged by the wealthy and the powerful. Jesus certainly knew this lesson. Do our actions match our own words? Do we land on the side of the powerful, or do we bend to the will of God who sides with those being wronged?

3 Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

4 Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.

5 Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.

6 Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled.

7 Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy.

8 Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.

9 Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.

10 Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. (Matt 5:3–10 NRSV)





1. See Jörg Jeremias, “Tradition und Redaktion in Micha 3,” in Verbindungslinien: Festschrift für Werner H. Schmidt zum 65. Geburtstag, ed. Axel Graupner, Holger Delkurt, and Alexander B. Ernst (Neukirchen-Vluyn: Neukirchener, 2000), 137–38. Jeremias argues that the chapter is increasingly seen as a single composition rather than the compilation of three independent units. He sees the call to attention in 3:1a and 3:9a as an inclusio that artistically helps create a frame (3:1–4, 9–12) around the divine speech in 3:5–8. Simultaneously, the judgment summary of 3:11 is directed not only against the politicians in 3:9–12, but also against those prophets mentioned within the middle section (3:5–7).

2. See Jeremias, 158. Jeremias astutely observes that 3:1–4 and 3:9–10 require one another to be fully comprehensible.

3. Old Testament scholars have recognized this diachronic break since early in the twentieth century. While scholars in the early twentieth century debated whether this opening word represented a scribal corruption, textual discoveries of early manuscripts in the middle of the twentieth century confirmed the presence of wāʾōmar. See Karl Budde, “Micha 2 und 3,” ZAW 38 (1920): 2–22, esp. 6–7, DOI: 10.1515/zatw.1920.38.1.2. After scholars began to understand the significance of these manuscripts, discussion largely shifted to the question of how to explain the role of this word, with most now recognizing that it originally functioned as a continuation of 2:6–11, as Budde had noted as early as 1921.

4. This judgment oracle structure is not as disrupted as Wagenaar claims. His desire to relocate 3:2b after 3:3 and to move 3:5aα in front of 3:2b as an introduction to the judgment appears contrived. Jan A. Wagenaar, “‘You Eat the Flesh of My People and Break Their Bones’: The Reversal of Fortunes in the Judgement Oracle Micah 3:1–4,” OTE 14 (2001): 525–31.

5. See a more detailed analysis of mišpāṭ in Bo Johnson, “מִשׁפָט,” TDOT 9:86–98. Johnson (87) notes three meanings of the word: (1) judgment; (2) a matter under judgment; and (3) something a judge or other official determined as “right.”

6. See Jeremias, “Tradition und Redaktion in Micha 3,” 148–49.

7. In compositional terms, these links were most likely created by the editor who updated the introductory chapter. See the discussion of the development of Micah as a corpus in the introduction to this commentary.

8. Wagenaar provides a brief discussion of those who have interpreted the cannibal imagery as an indication of actual human sacrifice, but most assume the images are used metaphorically (Wagenaar, “You Eat the Flesh of My People,” 530). The context of the surrounding verses strongly suggests that the images should not be taken literally.

9. See Robert P. Carroll, “Night without Vision: Micah and the Prophets,” in The Scriptures and the Scrolls: Studies in Honor of A. S. van der Woude on the Occasion of His 65th Birthday, ed. Florentino García Martínez, Anthony Hilhorst, and Casper J. Labuschagne, VTSup 49 (Leiden: Brill, 1992), 74–84. Carroll objects to the facile use of this phrase, arguing false prophets is too generic a categorization but that attention must be paid to the specific rationale regarding why one prophet condemns another. He correctly notes that Micah condemns these prophets for tying their message to the willingness of listeners to pay.

10. Scholars are divided on whether 3:5–8 represents an independent oracle placed here for effect or functions as an integral piece of a larger composition. Recent scholarship has tended to support the latter as illustrated by Utzschneider, Jeremias, and Allen. Utzschneider (80–81) sees 3:5–8 as an integral part of 3:1–8, while 3:9–12 picks up phrases from the extended context of chs. 1–3. Jeremias (158–59) argues that the entire chapter has been created to be read as a single unit. Allen (304) sees the entire chapter as a unit with three stanzas, held together by the word justice that appears in each stanza. By contrast, Wolff (92) acknowledges Mic 3 is a unit, but he also sees it as compiled of three different rhetorical units. Mays (76–92) essentially treats the three parts as independent units, which he labels as sayings, though he also presumes that the prophet himself is the one who ordered the sayings.

11. Jeremias emphasizes the role of intercession and draws out several typical reasons people would consult prophets, including economic and political emergencies (Jeremias, “Tradition und Redaktion in Micha 3,” 146).

12. At this point, one should take issue with attempts to theologize this passage as a means of assessment of competing theological claims. Jennifer K. Berenson MacLean, “Micah 3:5–12,” Int 56 (2002): 413–16, DOI: 10.1177/002096430005600408. Such approaches weaken the connection between the Bible, theology, and life. Micah’s powerful condemnation does not want to be taken as one voice among many but realizes the human cost of the brutal treatment of one group by another.

13. March, “Prophecy,” 160.

14. See Innocent Himbaza, “‘Se couviront-ils la moustache?’ (Michée 3:7),” BN 88 (1997): 27–30.

15. Gerstenberger notes just how unusual this type of comparison is within prophetic literature with the exception of Mic 1–3, where it appears in 1:8–9 and 2:11. Erhard S. Gerstenberger, “Kritik an Autoritäten (Mi 3,9–12),” BK 51 (1996): 161.

16. A substantial number of commentators consider the phrase ʾet rûaḥ yhwh as an explanatory gloss that was added to make explicit what was implicit, that the strength about which the prophet speaks is the strength that comes from Yahweh. The word ʾet is either the direct object marker or the preposition meaning “with.” I have translated it “with” to accentuate the fact that only this phrase has ʾet while the other three words must be treated as objects of the verb mlʾ (“to be full of”). As most note, the phrase ʾet rûaḥ yhwh breaks the poetic rhythm of the verse, creates an awkward syntactical sentence, and contains an extraneous direct object marker or preposition. See, e.g., Wolff, 91–92; Smith-Christopher, 119; Jeremias, 157, 164. Other commentators do not even note the possibility, essentially refusing to speculate on whether this was a later addition or not (Smith, 32–33). Others reject the need to see the line as a later expansion because they translate ʾet as the preposition (“with”); e.g., Johannes Lindblom, Prophecy in Ancient Israel (Oxford: Blackwell, 1962), 175; Allen, 314. In my opinion, the extraneous ʾet on the second of four objects sets this phrase apart in a way that would be typical of marginal glosses, but Wolff and others correctly note that the gloss does not really change the meaning. It merely clarifies the type of strength that fills Micah.

17. Carroll correctly notes that this phrase is not tied exclusively to prophets and Mic 3:8 focuses upon the selling of prophecy for money, but contra Carroll, the context does suggest that Mic 3:8 does challenge prophets who do otherwise (Carroll, “Night without Vision,” 76–79).

18. Gerstenberger, “Kritik an Autoritäten,” 160.

19. See Mark E. Biddle, Missing the Mark: Sin and Its Consequences in Biblical Theology (Nashville: Abingdon, 2005), 16–74. Biddle discusses both aspects of sin in these pages from a larger biblical perspective.

20. The terms Jacob and Israel are here used as synonyms (Gerstenberger, “Kritik an Autoritäten,” 160).

21. See Jeremias, 165.

22. Some scholars demur from interpreting 3:9–12 too exclusively with the events surrounding the attack of Sennacherib in 701 because the oracle could have been framed any time after Samaria’s destruction (Wolff, 95–97; Jeremias, 317; Mays, 88). Allen (243, cf. 305–6) takes a slightly different track by dating them before 701 but sees the time as one of “external calm and national security.” Allen’s explanation fails to account for the fact that following the rebellion of Ashdod, Hezekiah was preoccupied with defending territory from the Philistines and shoring up defenses in the Shephelah.

23. See Johnson, “mišpāṭ,” 92–93; and Helmer Ringgren and Louis Alonso-Schökel, “יָשַׁר,” TDOT 6:463–72, esp. 466–67.

24. Text critically, it is difficult to determine whether the original text read bnh with the MT or bny as reflected in the Greek tradition. Nevertheless, the use of bny fits the context better since it would be a masculine plural construct.

25. See the discussion of the expansion of Jerusalem under Hezekiah followed by significant loss of territory in the latter part of his reign in Klaus Bieberstein, A Brief History of Jerusalem: From the Earliest Settlement to the Destruction of the City in AD 70, ADPV 47 (Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, 2017), 59–78.

26. Several scholars take note of the fact that Hezekiah is credited with building the tunnel that brought Jerusalem’s water source inside the city gates (see 2 Kgs 20:20; 2 Chr 32:30; see also Utzschneider, 81). This action appears to involve preparation for military attacks on Jerusalem. In addition, the material findings of the so-called lmlk jars generated debates about their association with Hezekiah’s preparations for war against Assyria. E.g., Smith-Christopher (14–15) emphasizes the eighth-century BCE date of the jars and their heavy saturation in fortress towns in the western foothill towns. He cites the analysis by Ussishkin, who argues that these jars contained wine and oil and would have been used for feeding troops. David Ussishkin, “Royal Judean Storage Jars and Private Seal Impressions,” BASOR 223 (1976): 1–13. Smith-Christopher dismisses the later assessment of Oded Lipschits, “Archaeological Facts, Historical Speculations and the Date of the LMLK Storage Jars: A Rejoinder to David Ussishkin,” JHebS 12.4 (2012): 1–16, DOI: 10.5508/jhs.2012.v12.a4. Lipschits has a stronger argument, however, when he claims that the lmlk storage jars were part of a much larger administrative structure than Ussishkin or Smith-Christopher wishes to acknowledge. Lipschits makes a persuasive case that Lachish was the location of the first collection center for Judean royal storage jars and that Ramat Raḥel became the administrative collection center after 701 when Lachish was destroyed. The storage jars at Lachish were those that appear in early versions of these jars while the jars with concentric circles and rosettes appear after 701. The early forms predate Hezekiah’s revolt against the Assyrians.

27. See Jeremias, 165; Mays, 90–91.

28. Allen, 317; Jeremias, 317; Mays, 88; Wolff, 106–7; Utzschneider, 81.

29. Sweeney, 2:374.

30. For background on this figure, see James D. Nogalski, The Book of the Twelve: Micah–Malachi, SHBC (Macon, GA: Smyth & Helwys, 2011), 515. The term Zion in 3:10 likely does not evoke this tradition directly since the parallelism and the presence of vocabulary point back to ch. 1, but the richness of Zion as a poetic image means one should not merely pass over the term as an exact synonym for Jerusalem.

31. See fuller discussions in Jeremias, “Tradition und Redaktion in Micha 3,” 148–49.

32. John A. Emerton, VTSup 43 (Leiden: Brill, 1991), 182–84. He presents compelling arguments that the Shaphanide tradents of Jeremiah had access to an early version of Micah traditions, which Hardmeier interprets as a reception of Micah in the post-Josiah years prior to Jerusalem’s destruction.
